Shtern and P. Shtern, states that for every finite subset $F \subset S$, the embedding dimension of $(F,d)$ into a Hilbert space must be no greater than the genus of $S$. In this work, we demonstrate that this condition is sufficient for any intrinsic metric on $S$. Our approach primarily utilizes a recent generalization of the Toponogov theorem regarding geodesic triangles in metric spaces with non-positive curvature. Furthermore, as a secondary result, we prove that when $S$ is compact, the condition becomes necessary and sufficient even for semi-normed spaces. Additionally, we examine specific cases involving trees and other trees adjacent to a hyperbolic space. A similar criterion, applicable to both Hilbert spaces and general semi-normed spaces, is provided for negative curvature. Topological constraints are also discussed; notably, if $S$ is a complete, non-positively curved space where every closed geodesic is removable, a negative curvature condition holds if and only if such spaces admit an isometric embedding into a Hilbert space. This particular condition serves as a generalization of a condition first introduced by J. Chepoi and I. Gavoille. Finally, this work addresses questions 9.9 and 9.10 from Y. Shen's list. Y. Shen had previously proven that the condition is sufficient under additional assumptions: either the space is universally elliptic, or it excludes certain obstructions such as a loop formed by a geodesic arc, a bi-infinite geodesic line, or a geodesic circle. Universal ellipticity constitutes another sufficient condition. The current paper extends the scope to other metric spaces. (Author's abstract)

We address two core issues: (1) consistency, which ensures that always-satisfiable instances always possess a legal mapping to the source, and (2) full entailment, which identifies all possible valid repairs. Our primary contribution is a decidability result for full entailability, applicable to sources with any schema and RDF targets constrained by nested ShEx (supporting RDFS, SHACL, and ShEx) that are guaranteed to be consistent. Additionally, we demonstrate that while finding a certification for existence entailability is generally undecidable due to the presence of right-uniqueness in EAV schemas, it remains decidable for practical subsets of ShEx. The problem of full entailability is EXPTIME-hard, whereas certification for existence entailability is 2EXPTIME-complete. Furthermore, the data exchange problem itself is undecidable for sources with RDFS schemas and RDF targets featuring nested ShEx constraints. All proposed algorithms utilize a novel approach termed nested nested certification, which represents right-joining of certified QBEs. This is achieved by either directly certifying QBEs or by utilizing existing QBE certifications for subqueries. The resulting schema-free algorithms do not rely on pre-computed sources of dependency information. Finally, we outline a pathway for adapting these techniques to Datalog targets. The concept of nested nested certification is grounded in nested certification, a technique previously employed to achieve decidability for existence certification in data exchange from relational sources to ordered Datalog targets. Our results represent the first application of nested certification to produce a decision procedure for certification in relational-to-RDF exchange, even in the absence of updates. Conversely, models trained on small datasets typically fail to learn relational knowledge without transfer learning from large corpora. This paper introduces an enhanced method for transferring semantic relations from multilingual context models, building upon the work of H\"{o}fling et al. (2021). Specifically, we modify the selection of linguistic units used for alignment and relation learning. Unlike previous approaches that align sentences, we align individual relation instances. Similarly, while earlier methods predicted relations from entire aligned sentences, we propose a novel update rule for the relation classifier that utilizes the alignments of individual instances. Empirical results demonstrate that our technique outperforms several recent baseline methods on four English binary classification tasks related to semantic knowledge. This study presents spectroscopic observations of five metal-rich B-type stars located in open clusters—two of which previously lacked spectral data. We classified all five stars as Be-types, supporting the hypothesis that supergiant clusters host a higher frequency of these objects compared to clusters with lower giant populations. Our analysis indicates that the excess emission in these stars is likely caused by coeval, post-main-sequence, disc-driven evolution, although we acknowledge that other formation channels, such as mass loss from a Be supergain or transition from a binary to single-star status, cannot be entirely excluded. Additionally, we identified a star with a high metal abundance and strong emission lines, marking the first known HgMn star exhibiting hydrogen excess. Finally, we utilized the derived stellar parameters to calculate the rate of Be-type stars in clusters with giant populations exceeding 1%, finding it to be approximately 1 in 1000. This result is 20 to 40 times greater than rates observed in globular clusters and roughly 10 times higher than those in the field. These findings align with current hypotheses regarding the primary role of disc-driven evolution in the formation of Be-type stars. Furthermore, the ratio of Be-type stars to red supergains in clusters with many giant stars is estimated at 1 in 10,000, consistent with theoretical models of post-main-sequence evolution. This ratio is significantly higher than in the Galactic field, providing additional support for clusters with giant populations as a key environment for Be supergains. In the context of stellar evolution, these findings suggest that the core contraction phase in post-red supergain stars may be the dominant pathway for Be supergains. Additionally, the ratio of Be supergains to red supergains in clusters remains at least an order of magnitude lower than the rate of red supergains undergoing binary transition or losing mass in the field. In this work, we extend the concept of GCM to GCRC matrices, which offer the ability to achieve omnidirectional beamforming. Leveraging the property of row orthogonality, we derive the necessary conditions for constructing GCM and identify an existing family of such matrices. Furthermore, by utilizing a standard method for generating Hadamard matrices, we derive a family of binary GCMs. Finally, we demonstrate the application of GCRCs in omnidirectional precoding, showing that these matrices help ensure fair channel conditions and minimize outage probability. Additionally, the orthogonal row structure of GCRC enables the design of low-complexity receivers based on zero-forcing techniques. Numerical simulations confirm that employing GCRC enables achievable rates to approach the input-output mutual information. Our proposed scheme also supports the blind identification of GCM, enhancing robustness against parameter estimation errors. These features highlight that GCM is a promising tool for future wireless communication systems. As a final note, we provide applications of GCM to Golay complementary sequences (GCS), demonstrating how to generate infinite families of GCS from a single pair using a cascade of GCM. Simulations indicate that GCS can outperform orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) by reducing both the mean square error of channel estimation and the outage probability. Furthermore, a GCM-based receiver with lower complexity than OFDM can be employed for GCS. Consequently, GCM holds value for wireless communication applications. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed GCM can be integrated into non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) to ensure equitable rate allocation among users. We also propose an enhanced version of the GCM-based precoder that, when combined with successive interference cancellation, yields improved performance. This method recasts the standard axioms of quantum mechanics to eliminate probabilistic and nonlocal elements, labeling the resulting theory as superdeterministic. A key feature of this framework is that it permits measurement settings to vary randomly, thereby distinguishing it from superdeterministic conspiracies. Although superdeterminism was long considered an obscure and unlikely concept, the emergence of quantum entanglement and quantum information theory has brought it into sharp focus. Furthermore, it is noted that superdeterminism is not limited to quantum mechanics but can be applied to any mathematical or physical theory, including determinantal quantum field theories. Functionally Safe systems operating in critical areas such as automotive and industrial environments rely on real-time execution to prevent accidents, injuries, and system damage. However, the rise of connected and electrified vehicles challenges these systems, as non-deterministic events from external sources can disrupt real-time execution. To ensure safety in such settings, systems often employ redundant, heterogeneous processors running distinct software versions, a configuration known as Triple-Modular Redundancy (TMR). This approach typically involves a majority-voting arbiter that can detect and isolate faults. Nevertheless, modern design trends are shifting away from TMR due to its high cost, reduced performance, and increased memory usage. Our proposed architecture utilizes a single processor to handle all functions, protected by an arbiter that monitors and isolates errors. This design offers a more practical path toward real-time achievement with greater cost-effectiveness, performance, and memory efficiency. It is particularly well-suited for non-critical real-time applications, including infotainment and driver assistance systems. We have implemented this design on an FPGA using an Industry Standard Serial (ISSD) interface (specifically the A-SIG standard), making it readily adaptable for System-on-Chip (SoC) integration. Furthermore, arbiter experiments demonstrate that the proposed design outperforms TMR by achieving 2.5 times higher performance, a 50% lower cost, and 30% savings in power consumption. Additionally, this solution supports Non-Intrusive Real-Time Analysis (NIRTA), allowing system integrators to measure real-time indicators like response time and real-time index post-deployment without modifying the system code or introducing measurement overhead. Finally, validation confirms the feasibility of the design in Automotive Grade computing environments. This research contributes to the broader goal of eliminating hard real-time systems for time-critical applications in cars, enabling developers to focus on other priorities. For bipartite states, it approximates the mutual information $I(A:C)$, making its study essential for understanding the structure of entanglement in quantum systems. This work investigates the reflected entropy $R$ associated with the most mixed pure states of matter fields within five-dimensional global AdS spaces, specifically those possessing matter spherical symmetry. Utilizing Fefferman-Graham expansions, we derive the asymptotic behavior of $R$ as a function of the entanglement region boundaries. Our findings demonstrate that the leading order term of $R$ exhibits additivity under partitioning of the subsystem, a characteristic shared with mutual information, thereby reinforcing the interpretation of reflected entropy as a proxy for mutual information in AdS/CFT contexts. Furthermore, we observe that for non-extremal black holes in global AdS, the EWCS comprises both bulk and boundary components, whereas in thermal AdS scenarios, it is determined solely by the boundary segment. These findings align with prior research conducted in asymptotically flat settings. Overall, our results underscore the efficacy of employing boundary approximations for EWCS within the AdS/CFT paradigm. Additionally, we explicitly confirm the inequality $I(A:B) \leq I(A:X) + I(A:Y)$ for the reflected entropy of spherical symmetric states in global AdS$_5$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings regarding the entanglement structure of quantum systems across different temperatures in the high-temperature limit. We demonstrate that the temperature dependence of the EWCS shares the same additivity property as the high-temperature limit, thereby substantiating the interpretation of reflected entropy as a proxy for mutual information within the AdS/CFT framework. This approach is applicable not only to thermal AdS but also to various other scenarios, including Einstein dilute black holes and black holes situated in dilute matter backgrounds. Our analysis further reveals that these features are not contingent upon the specific dimensionality of the asymptotic space, remaining valid across diverse dimensions. Consequently, this methodology offers a robust and versatile tool for analyzing the entanglement structures of quantum systems in higher dimensions. Consequently, the methods employed in this paper can be extended to examine reflected entropy and mutual information in higher dimensions, providing a valuable resource for future investigations into the entanglement structures of quantum systems across different temperatures. We model this process using Mott transition times, which are derived from decoherence rates in open quantum systems that cannot be described by the standard Hamiltonian system. Our findings indicate that these rates are proportional to the barrier's thickness, demonstrating that quantum Mott tunneling does not violate the classical speed limit. In the limit of an infinitely thick barrier, classical physics emerges, and the associated velocity equals the minimum group delay—often mistakenly referred to as tunneling time—calculated for lower-energy particles within the barrier. Although our specific model may not universally apply, it effectively addresses numerous experimental scenarios, including those involving superconducting qubits and nanomechanical resonators. These systems are typically analyzed using standard formalisms, yet their results can be more intuitively understood through Mott tunneling. This nuanced perspective may prove valuable for deciphering data from experiments on tunneling, delay times, decoherence, energy conservation violations, and measurements related to the anomalous Casimir effect. Notably, open quantum systems exhibit all five known Mott tunneling mechanisms, which correspond to various established models for tunneling time. Our results suggest that these models, representing different manifestations of Mott tunneling, may possess distinct physical meanings. Ultimately, these insights contribute to a clearer comprehension of the fundamental mechanisms underlying quantum tunneling. Allergy diagnosis typically involves an in-person clinical visit where patients undergo interviews and in-vivo intradermal skin testing, a process that is both resource-intensive and difficult to scale. In contrast, telemedicine offers a more accessible and scalable alternative for remote patient assessment. This study introduces a non-invasive method utilizing computer vision to analyze facial expressions and determine allergic sensitization. Specifically, we developed a deep convolutional neural network trained on a annotated dataset of actor performances of tick and other allergen allergic reactions. This computer vision technique serves as a surrogate for intradermal testing and demonstrates promising results in distinguishing between true allergies and misconceptions. Furthermore, the proposed method and computer vision framework can be easily generalized to other allergens by retraining the network with corresponding performance data. Ultimately, this represents a significant advancement in non-invasive, remote diagnostic capabilities. By integrating an PID controller and a PFC within a network model featuring PIDs, PFCs, inertial loads, frequency-dependent active power, synchronous generators, heat rate curves, frequency-dependent active power losses, and second-order inertial loads, we derive the nonlinear nonlinear differential-algebraic equations governing IFS. Following the linearization of these nonlinear equations, we transform them into a linear, time-invariant, nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations. Based on this mathematical model, we develop a new methodology to determine the stability boundaries of IFS. Numerical results demonstrate that PID controllers combined with conventional PFCs can significantly enhance the IFS stability region compared to standard PID controllers, with the optimal PFC design being one possessing an integral gain of zero. However, it is also found that PFCs utilizing PIDs may fail to further expand the IFS stability region when operating with PID controllers lacking angular velocity damping. These findings offer valuable design insights for network operators, specifically regarding the parameters of network frequency controllers and PFCs. \section*{I. Introduction}

Over the past few decades, significant progress has been made in understanding soft matter systems, with recent focus shifting toward active matter. This category encompasses a wide range of materials, including self-propelled particles, bacterial colonies, and biological tissues. A prominent example is the \textit{active matter} model, which consists of self-propelled particles moving with constant velocity in a random direction, with velocity fluctuating at random intervals. These systems have been extensively studied both theoretically and experimentally. However, most existing research assumes particles are spherical or elongated with rotational rigidity. Despite this, it is well-documented that particles in real-world environments possess non-zero angle rigidity. To date, however, studies on angle-rigid active matter remain limited.

We introduce a process tomography technique based on shadow tomography, which substantially reduces the count of post-selected measurements, thereby minimizing the impact of statistical fluctuations. Additionally, we present a novel method to mitigate bias caused by post-selection in this context, which also enhances performance for standard tomographic schemes. We evaluated our results on randomly generated noisy quantum processes using randomly selected input and output states, as well as on experimentally realized unitary processes characterized by varying degrees of noise. Furthermore, we validated our findings on actual quantum hardware from IBM QX, Rigaku QCS, and QuTech D-Wave, which were impacted by gate noise, qubit decoherence, and readout noise. Our findings indicate that the proposed shadow tomography scheme is robust against imperfections in experimental hardware, offering significant improvements over conventional tomography even in highly noisy environments. We expect this approach to be vital for systematically mapping noise in noisy quantum hardware, a requirement for advancing quantum information processing. An external perpendicular magnetic field opens a Landau level (LL) spectrum featuring a prominent zeroth LL located at the Dirac point, along with distinct linearly dispersing electron bands in the very low-energy region. In this work, we investigate the charge imbalance and magnetization of these linear bands under a magnetic field. Using the random phase approximation (RPA), we calculate a non-monotonic phase diagram for the charge imbalance. Notably, without trigonal warping, a charge imbalance phase diagram emerges even without trigonal flux, a finding that contrasts with the established behavior in monolayer graphene. This theoretical prediction is experimentally testable, as relevant systems have already been realized, providing motivation for its re-examination. Furthermore, we also examine the magnetization of these linear bands within the presence and absence of trigonal warping. These findings offer a theoretical basis for the potential observation of magnetic ordering in graphene. Additionally, our analysis of magnetization in the absence of trigonal warping and trigonal flux, combined with the predicted charge imbalance, provides a pathway to achieve the charge-ordered phase, serving as an alternative explanation for the charge density wave observed in magic-angle graphene. Finally, we also explore the magnetization related to the giant LL associated with trigonal warping and its subsequent experimental verification. Our study on trigalwarping therefore offers a fresh perspective on recent experimental findings. In summary, the theoretical results presented here provide valuable insights for future experiments on trilayer graphene systems. Furthermore, our findings may offer inspiration for researching magnetism in single- and few-layer graphene. Focusing on charge imbalance, the proposed mechanism could offer a fresh perspective on the charge ordered phase phenomenon, potentially advancing the exploration of charge ordering in graphene. Finally, our analysis of trigonal warping provides a new angle for understanding recent experimental results. To achieve this, we also offer an explanation for a foraminifera. In parameter-dependent dephasing channels, however, the channel generator's dependence on the parameter prevents the straightforward application of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) lower bound found in the constant dephasing case. We demonstrate that when dephasing is weak, utilizing optimal states enables the QBI to closely approximate the constant dephasing scenario. Furthermore, within the short-time regime, we show that for specific parameter-dependent dephasing channels, both the QFI upper and lower bounds converge to the same value as in the constant dephasing situation. These findings offer practical insights for implementing quantum phase estimation under various noise conditions. Additionally, we illustrate that under global dephasing, the QFI upper bound equals the lower bound during the short-time approximation of the Bose-Meissner-Pauli expansion. This allows the QFI to be effectively estimated by analyzing the quantum Cramér-Rao bound of the parameter-dependent Hamiltonian alongside the trace norm of the relative density matrix difference. Finally, we examine the quantum Cramér-Rao bound for the Ramsey sequence under constant dephasing noise, comparing the performance of the bright phase estimation strategy against the dark one. Our results indicate that for short-time constant dephasing noise, the thermodynamic Fisher information (TFI) for the Ramsey sequence can be approximately calculated by considering the TFI of the parameter-dependent Hamiltonian. These findings significantly facilitate quantum phase estimation. Focusing on the case where dephasing is caused by thermal fluctuations, we employ the thermodynamic formalism of dissipation to derive an explicit expression for the TFI as a function of the environment's temperature. This highlights the trade-off between precision and environmental temperature, demonstrating how thermal properties of the environment influence the TFI of the Ramsey sequence. Consequently, our findings provide valuable guidance for conducting quantum phase estimation. Nevertheless, its utility is constrained by the substantial number of quantum operations needed to assess individual terms within Hamiltonian interactions. This limitation becomes particularly severe in superconducting quantum processors, where such operations are hindered by extended circuit depths and significant noise. To address this, we present a novel approach utilizing in situ machine learning to accelerate VQE convergence. Our method reframes the VQE process as a series of regression tasks, involving a quantum circuit that generates quantum data and a classical optimizer that optimizes circuit parameters. By applying machine learning to execute both the circuit and parameter optimization, we circumvent multiple iterations and reduce the total number of evaluations. We validate this technique across two distinct models: a Heisenberg ferromagnet and a hydrogen molecule. Our approach demonstrates that it can match or surpass the efficiency of traditional VQE methods in achieving convergence for these examples. In conclusion, our findings indicate that an ML-enhanced VQE framework can significantly expedite the determination of the ground state energy expectation value. This paves the way for developing more robust quantum eigensolvers, even when utilizing noisy, near-term hardware. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have proven highly effective for modeling word distributions, previous attempts to incorporate temporal context into deep generative models of language have largely overlooked the decay of activation values over time and the distinct roles played by different activation levels, limiting their ability to capture the full dynamics of sentence production. To address this, we introduce the DecayNet and the Heterogeneous DecayNet—deep generative models that explicitly simulate temporal dynamics within sentences. These architectures utilize decay rates and other parameters to jointly model the timing and values of word occurrences. Furthermore, we propose integrating sentence-level and word-level distributions to create more nuanced models, as evidenced by superior character-level perplexity results (Pig-19,138,118). Additionally, these methods enhance the robustness of downstream tasks; at minimum, they mitigate biases in part-of-speech tagging when used as pretrained features with Word2Vec, achieving only marginal performance shifts in most instances. Finally, our framework offers a framework for analyzing sentence dynamics that is complementary to the statistical methods currently dominant in natural language processing. These findings pave the way for unified models capable of handling varying degrees of dynamism in language and temporal phenomena across different domains. (MO-MINLP) problems are a significant challenge in mathematical programming, particularly within process engineering. This domain frequently involves scenarios where engineering goals must be balanced against environmental consequences. A prominent example is the trade-off between energy consumption and CO2 emissions within a chemical production facility. This article introduces a computational case study based on a supra-structure designed to model a generic industrial plant. By applying bilevel convexification, we transform the MO-MINLP into a sequence of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problems. To generate a Pareto-optimal solution set for the reformed model, we integrate the adaptive large neighbourhood search heuristic AMPLIA with an adaptive large neighbourhood exact search algorithm. We demonstrate that this algorithmic sequence successfully produces a collection of Pareto-optimal solutions for the plant supra-structure MO-MINLP. Furthermore, these solutions highlight a clear compromise between reduced energy usage and lower CO2 emissions. All algorithms presented in this study are implemented in Python and are available as open-source under the Apache License 2.0. We utilize the Pyomo framework for formulating models and solving the optimization problems. All Pyomo components, including the added contributions, are released as open-source under the same license. Additionally, employing an object-oriented framework like Pyomo facilitates the straightforward extension of the model. This work presents a foundational step toward utilizing AI and Machine Learning in the context of MO-MINLP problems. Such an approach could further enhance the quality of the resulting solution sets. Our code repository incorporates machine learning and artificial intelligence libraries to support this objective, all of which are provided as open-source. Every component requires a minor adjustment to the code to align with the overarching goal, which is to establish a framework for applying AI and ML to MO-MINLP problems. All elements are released as open-source under the Apache License 2.0. The designed algorithm relies on a partial convexification of the non-convex problem, utilizing the majorization-minimization approach. Finally, the scheme exhibits low sensitivity to the number of RIS elements, enabling effective communication even with a modest number of RIS assets. These outcomes are anticipated to facilitate the integration of this technique into the WSA 6G framework. Within the context of quantum thermodynamics, we investigate the steady-state entanglement produced by the continuous measurement and damping of multi-mode optomechanical oscillators. Our key finding reveals that while $q$-deformation enhances mechanical photon numbers, it simultaneously suppresses both the entropy of state and the degree of entanglement. These findings underscore the intricate relationship between information and energy as macroscopic oscillators approach classical behavior, and suggest that $q$-deformation plays a pivotal role in experimental endeavors to generate and sustain macroscopic entanglement. Furthermore, our results offer valuable theoretical guidance for designing hybrid quantum devices capable of measuring and damping multi-mode optomechanical oscillators. Additionally, our study addresses the debate surrounding whether quantum mechanics can be formulated without reference to time. We demonstrate that the Bell-like inequality remains invariant under time-reversal, thereby affirming that time in quantum theory possesses an entropic nature. Finally, within the framework of stochastic thermodynamics, our results indicate that the quantum thermodynamic law applicable to $q$-deformed optomechanical oscillators maintains the same form as in standard quantum mechanics, even when $q\neq 1$. These outcomes may contribute to a comprehensive understanding of quantum thermodynamics, information theory, and the foundational nature of time. This basic feedforward neural network is trained to fit cell averages of a partial differential equation (PDE) solution, with specific examples demonstrating its capacity to accurately approximate PDE solutions over extended periods. We demonstrate error-free propagation over exponentially long durations for both linear advection and the Burgers equation. Furthermore, we propose a theory showing that the network's error bounds depend on training data size and dimensionality rather than the initial condition or time horizon. This indicates that the network learns general features of the underlying PDE, enabling accurate predictions even for initial conditions not present in the training set. We also present evidence suggesting the network captures PDE behavior at a rate exponentially faster than standard finite volume methods. Finally, we explore extensions of these error bounds to systems of PDEs, nonlinear advection, and boundary value problems. All proposed methods are validated through numerical experiments. We argue that this error bound analysis and theoretical results can guide future neural network designs aimed at solving PDEs. The proposed network represents a new framework for PDE approximation, capable of arbitrary-order accuracy, free from spatial discretization artifacts, and largely independent of the initial condition or time horizon. Its exceptional error bounds, generalization capabilities, and lack of discretization artifacts make it highly promising for scientific computing and other real-world applications. By applying the Rindler interpretation of the Unruh effect to light-cone coordinates, we demonstrate that thermal fluctuations in the past light cone lead to hysteresis within both dissipative and conservative systems, thereby confirming its validity. This thermalization through light-cone correlations can be seen as the fundamental mechanism, with the Rindler wedge serving as one specific manifestation of this phenomenon within a broader context. We offer concrete examples involving hysteresis in dissipative systems and elastic waves to validate the effect. These findings hold relevance for gravitational wave observatories and scenarios where past light-cone correlations are significant. Furthermore, we illustrate the phenomenon using a simple model of an accelerating charge, showing that the radiated energy from the past light cone creates historical radiation reaction forces. Additionally, classical electron dynamics provide a natural explanation for the principle behind our proposed principle. Based on this, we present several experiments to detect the light-cone induced light-cone effect (LCCLE). Our predictions suggest that the size of the LCCLE during an interferometric measurement is more readily detectable in high-reflectivity cavities using pulsed lasers, with the pulse duration and beam waist being critical tuning parameters. The magnitude of the LCCLE is expected to be of the order of $10^{-18}$ meters, which is more than ten orders of magnitude larger than any quantum effect, making it potentially observable in current or future interferometric experiments at gravitational wave observatories. Consequently, we propose a novel framework for understanding gravitational wave signals generated by charge distributions in space. This work can be viewed as a theoretical experiment that may guide practical research and measurements to explore and investigate the LCCLE. Our analysis of gravitational wave signals from charged distributions in space may provide new insights and alternative explanations for the signals detected by gravitational wave observatories. In this context, we have developed a new perspective and introduced corresponding terminology. The theoretical and experimental implications of the LCCLE are discussed. It is anticipated that this contribution will inspire experimental efforts to verify the LCCLE using existing or upgraded facilities of gravitational wave observatories. Most current research focuses on the Task A phase of event extraction, which involves defining templates and labeling the text. Recently, Template Extraction (Task B)—the process of generating templates from unlabeled, real-world text—has gained attention for creating robust IE systems tailored to specific domains. This paper investigates these relationships by exploring the potential of using Template Extraction to enhance standard IE systems. This jet formation relies on the Blandford-Znajek effect, which requires the black hole's spin to be tapped by rotating magnetic fields. We demonstrate that current MHD simulations fail to produce jets because they employ frozen-in boundary conditions at the black hole horizon. In reality, however, the horizon's conductive properties, as described by general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD), create an additional boundary condition that significantly influences jet dynamics. Utilizing force-free electrodynamics (FFE) jet simulations, we show that inserting a magnetic membrane at the black hole horizon—representing the conductive horizon—dramatically enhances the jets when compared to models where the horizon is treated as a Cauchy boundary. Furthermore, we illustrate that a GRMHD magnetosheath model can be approximated by this magnetic membrane. Consequently, we advocate the implementation of an appropriate magnetic membrane model in MHD simulations to accurately represent the essential role of horizon conductivity in these systems. Finally, we provide an analytical explanation for the jets' performance based on FFE theory and the black hole's spin extraction capabilities. We conclude that rapidly spinning black holes are predisposed to launch powerful jets due to the conductive nature of their horizons. We also examine how increasing the magnetic field strength within the accretion flow further amplifies the resulting jets. Historically, CPA involved stretching an ultrashort laser pulse in time, amplifying the stretched waveform, and then compressing it to retrieve the original peak intensity. While this description captures the essence of CPA, it fails to account for CPA configurations that utilize spatial or frequency domain stretching rather than temporal time-domain methods. This study enhances the factual consistency of text generated by large-scale pre-trained transformer models by introducing a two-stage framework. In the first stage, the initial output is refined to improve its factual alignment with the input context, a process guided by an alignment judge that identifies and corrects inconsistencies without requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning. The proposed scheme leverages the three key properties of RingCT: confidentiality, unlinkability, and validity. Delegated RingCT employs a randomization technique for all cryptographic operations to achieve generic zero-knowledge properties, thereby enhancing its resistance to the specific attacks targeted by DPoS consensus schemes. Additionally, the scheme utilizes a lightweight signature method for its cryptographic functions, facilitating efficient verification by third-party verifiers (TVs) within the DPoS framework. Performance evaluations demonstrate that the computational costs for the sender, TV, and validator are significantly lower in the proposed scheme compared to the Delegated IOTA framework. Furthermore, an analysis of function complexity reveals that the computational burden on the validator in the proposed scheme (excluding the TV) surpasses that of the Bitcoin protocol using the Schnorr signature. These results indicate that Delegated RingCT outperforms both the IOTA Delegated framework and Bitcoin, offering a more suitable solution for high-velocity transactions in high-performance DPoS blockchain environments. Large Hadron Collider (LHC) initiated a record-breaking run of high-energy physics operations at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This study analyzes a dataset of dielectron events from proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS detector during this run, with an integrated luminosity of 3.6 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis covers the range $2 < m_{ee} < 130$ GeV, where $m_{ee}$ denotes the invariant mass of the electron pair. No excess of electrons was detected, leading to exclusion limits at 95% confidence level for several new phenomena. These include a vector resonance decaying into on-shell Z bosons, with the Z subsequently decaying into on-shell Higgs bosons that further decay into on-shell $\tau$ lepton pairs; this yielded an upper bound on the production cross section times the double-tagged efficiency of $\sigma \times \epsilon$ of 0.44 fb at a production mass of 2.5 TeV. Additionally, limits were established for various scenarios involving the production of heavy virtual states. For Higgs boson pairs produced via vector boson fusion, the corresponding differential cross section (before applying efficiency corrections) is constrained to be less than 0.73 pb when both Higgs bosons decay into $\tau$ lepton pairs via their dominant channel. These findings complement recent experimental results regarding the rare decay of the Higgs boson into two $\tau$ lepton pairs.

We introduce a human evaluation study assessing the efficacy of three rejection criteria for text generation in English dialogue: three, 13-gram perplexity thresholds and three entropy thresholds. Our results indicate that while rejection rates remain low, suitable outputs are significantly more likely to be accepted than inappropriate ones. However, users struggle to distinguish between good and bad text, often relying on prior context rather than the generated dialogue itself. While current methods for detecting micro-seismic events typically rely on fixed template matching, these approaches are limited by their reliance on specific feature selection and the necessity for human expertise. This study employs a novel machine learning approach using template-free matching, where the signal template is absent. The method relies solely on the similarity between signal segments and the cross-correlation function between them. By calculating this function, the proposed templateless matching technique can identify micro-seismic events by analyzing fluctuations in the values. This paper presents the findings and validates the method through an application demonstrating its effectiveness. The results indicate that the templateless matching approach is highly effective for identifying micro-seismic events and holds potential for broader applications. Furthermore, the method proves particularly useful for tracking event locations, as it utilizes all features within the signal, rendering it independent of selected features and expert knowledge. Consequently, this enhances the method's stability and reliability. Additionally, since the process does not involve feature selection, the overall time complexity is significantly reduced. In summary, this paper introduces an expert-independent, stable, and robust templateless matching technique for seismic signal analysis. The method achieves 94% detection accuracy, surpasses existing approaches, and offers greater versatility across different seismic signals. Finally, the method demonstrates the capability to pinpoint event locations with high precision, achieving a location error of less than 10 meters. The methodology has been tested and validated on data from seismic stations in Sivas and Nizip, Turkey, utilizing events recorded between 2017 and 2019. A dataset comprising 10 micro-seismic events was analyzed to evaluate and compare the performance of both template-based and templateless matching methods. The results confirm that the templateless matching approach is effective for signal analysis and successfully identifies micro-seismic events. Additionally, the method exhibits superior performance in event localization, achieving a location error rate of less than 10 meters. Finally, the study demonstrates that the templateless matching method is more versatile than the template-based approach. The estimated generator yields exact estimates of fluorescence lifetime parameters, demonstrating accuracy even under high noise levels and during the prediction of time-resolved fluorescence responses for excitation wavelengths not present in the training data. A defining characteristic of these theories is the presence of a physical boundary or interface that prevents the system from achieving true ground states at asymptotic spatial infinities. Consequently, standard conformal blocks are insufficient for describing boundary and interface operators. Instead, operators situated on the boundary or within the system are represented by generalized conformal blocks featuring novel tensorial structures. For instance, in BCFT, a conformal block is defined by a tensor that contracts a spinor index with the indicator vectors of local operators. However, deriving the explicit formulation of these tensorial objects remains unresolved even in these basic scenarios. This work introduces the methodology for constructing conformal blocks by applying an algebraic classification to primary fields. By utilizing SHY tensors as an analogue for the spinor index of local operators, we derive the explicit formula for primary-primary (PP) tensors under various boundary and interface conditions. Furthermore, we examine primary-primary-primary (PPP) tensors across different configurations and provide the explicit expressions for these cases as well. This study serves as a foundational step toward elucidating the algebraic properties of BCFT and ICFT. The approaches and specific tensors presented here can also be extended to more complex scenarios, such as those involving stress-energy-primary-operator (TPO), stress-energy-stress-energy (TTE), or stress-energy-primary-operator-stress-energy (TPOST) correlation functions. Our results may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of boundary and interface correlations in these frameworks. Our derivations are based on established literature; therefore, while the computational process is systematic and does not rely on numerical approximations, potential inaccuracies could stem from human error. generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is essential for algorithms utilizing a local model to train, compress, or interpret deep neural networks. Current approaches to estimating the GGN's exact or stochastic sparse-structured linear approximation (SSLAP) rely on specific data-covariance assumptions, which often result in biased estimates. This paper investigates data-covariance assumptions derived from an analysis of backpropagation and presents Assumed Structure Gaussian Noise (ASGN), a novel, general algorithm that efficiently and accurately estimates the SSLAP of the GGN without relying on data-covariance assumptions. The proposed method is fully backpropagation-compatible, self-contained, and straightforward to implement. Experimental results demonstrate that ASGN serves as a reliable alternative to existing techniques.

We demonstrate that this phenomenon influences word representations, causing inanimate nouns with differing genders that lack semantic overlap to activate distinct concepts. Although previous studies have examined the gender system's impact on semantic representation and learning within the context of language expansion, gender biases have not yet been investigated in models trained solely on non-linguistic data. We gathered a gendered wordlist from 17 languages lacking a training corpus and employed it to assess whether gender biases exist in widely used pre-trained word embeddings. These biases manifest most prominently in inflectional paradigms of inanimate nouns and in the neighbor word distributions of inanimate nouns with distinct genders. These observations offer strong evidence that gender biases are inherent to word embeddings, which has significant implications for tasks involving language and vision, particularly regarding downstream tasks where models cannot disentangle gendered noise from task-specific features. Furthermore, we show that gender is captured in lower layers of ELMo representations, whereas gender-free representations like BERT already mitigate these biases. Finally, we propose gender sensitivity as a metric for evaluating representation models. Experimental results indicate that the ELMo and mBPE models exhibit reduced gender sensitivity compared to other models. Through case studies, we demonstrate the potential for automatically detecting gendered wordlist contamination in translation tasks using either model. In conclusion, these results suggest that gender biases in word embeddings are driven by linguistic data and can be minimized by utilizing gender-free representations or pre-trained models with fewer parameters. Both approaches maintain competitive performance on non-linguistic tasks. We release a GitHub repository containing all experiments and code necessary to replicate our results. electrical power systems, which rely on maintaining voltage and frequency within safe limits. Although extensive research has addressed frequency and voltage dynamics separately, their coupled effects on system stability remain underexplored. This study examines frequency and voltage coupled dynamics in two-phase networks, specifically within a high-voltage direct current (HVDC)-linked asynchronous power system (APS). Utilizing a detailed HVDC model, we derive linearized frequency and voltage dynamics for single-machine and multi-machine networks, subsequently developing large-scale frequency and voltage coupled models based on these system-level representations. Finally, we analyze how voltage dynamics influence frequency dynamics and the resulting system stability. Our findings indicate that neglecting frequency dynamics in ultra-high voltage networks can yield inaccurate assessments of frequency dynamics, with these effects intensifying under heavier loads. Furthermore, large-scale modeling reveals that ignoring coupled frequency and voltage dynamics eliminates critical frequency oscillation modes, potentially leading to unstable operation. This research contributes to enhancing the stability of electrical power systems by elucidating the interaction between frequency and voltage dynamics. Extensive numerical simulations confirm the validity of our analytical results. The proposed large-scale models and associated analysis are expected to be valuable for improving the stability of APSs, particularly in the design and operation of renewable energy-based electrical power systems. Specifically, these findings can aid in selecting appropriate controllers, determining optimal locations for renewable energy sources, and formulating effective operational strategies. While this study focuses on electric power systems, the methodology and conclusions are applicable to other multi-phasic systems, such as hydraulic drive systems, hydraulic-mechanical coupled systems, and mechanical-electrical coupled systems. In these contexts, established control and monitoring techniques for electrical power systems can be adapted; the derived linear and large-scale models and analysis results are transferable by substituting electrical power system variables with their respective counterparts in those other domains. Specifically, replacing electrical variables (voltage, current, power) with their hydraulic or mechanical equivalents allows the current methodology to be effectively applied to those related fields. **Methods.** Inspired by tomographic reconstruction algorithms, the nonlinear inversion procedure utilizes an iterative scheme. Starting from an initial model, each subsequent model is derived from the residuals of the previous one.

**Results.** The method was tested on synthetic data produced by three-dimensional (3D) ray-tracing simulations of acoustic wave packets within a realistic solar interior model. These packets were detected using Gaussian beam convolution. The resulting sound-speed profiles for both realistic and simplified background models closely matched the input profiles, exhibiting small systematic and random errors. Additionally, the packet injection model was reconstructed with reasonable accuracy.

**Conclusions.** The nonlinear inversion approach effectively recovers effective one-dimensional sound-speed profiles from synthetic acoustic wave packet travel-time data. This confirms that the method is viable for applying local helioseismology to estimate solar sound-speed profiles.

**Keywords:** Sun: interior, Local Helioseismology, methods: inversion

electron transport in molecular systems. It utilizes the Pararotnone Hamiltonian, which combines the phonon bath of a rigid molecule with the electronic ground and excited states of a localized orbital. Electron movement is simulated through off-diagonal reconfigurations of ground-state orbitals, while the phonon bath is simulated using the Debye model. Upon excitation of an electron, energy is transferred to the phonon bath. The resulting phonon-electron interaction shifts molecular vibrations toward lower frequencies and broadens the emission spectrum. Finally, various configurations of molecules are arranged to facilitate electron transport between them, creating pathways influenced by phonon-electron interactions and orientational disorder. The model successfully reproduces key experimental findings from charge-transfer salts featuring both frequent and rare pathways, specifically applying to 2,4,5-T and DCBTA molecules. In these salt configurations, electron transport exhibits signatures of percolation theory, characterized by power-law distributions of pathways and distinct variations in mobility anisotropy. These findings suggest that the broad emission lines observed in electron mobility measurements indicate strong phonon-electron coupling. Furthermore, the findings imply that the frequency dispersion of electron emission serves as a precise metric for phonon-electron coupling strength. Ultimately, this phonon-electron coupling creates bottlenecks in frequent pathways and traps electrons in infrequent ones, thereby driving the percolation observed in electron transport. These results provide critical insights for the development of organic electron transport materials. This study presents in-situ convective Rossby wave simulations conducted across three magnetic strength regimes. Utilizing a high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic model of the photosphere, we applied a spectral filter to gradually increase the Biot number ($Bi$), thereby suppressing convective velocities, before conducting a final purely hydrodynamic run to reconstruct the original flow. We employed the optimal control algorithm (OCA), which surpasses traditional machine learning methods, to achieve this. The results indicate that while the algorithm accurately restores flow velocities for $Bi<100$, the restoring capability diminishes as $Bi$ exceeds 100. Crucially, we demonstrate that the algorithm's failure to recover the flow is not due to the reduction in velocities. Instead, the loss of physical information from the original system correlates with the loss of magnetic field energy. These findings suggest that sunspot regions, characterized by high magnetic field strengths, cannot be accurately modeled using low magnetic potential values. Consequently, assuming that non-ideal effects are negligible in these regions is invalid. Furthermore, the proposed OCA method proves effective for handling MHD systems. Finally, we conclude that the deep learning model utilized in this research should be retrained using high-$Bi$ datasets to enhance its performance. We introduce a correction method for wide-field cameras equipped with on-board focal plane cameras. This approach utilizes images taken with off-axis patches to measure atmospheric dispersion and applies corrections directly within the focal plane before integration. A key feature of this paradigm is the radiative breaking of the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry at a scale significantly lower than the supersymmetry-breaking threshold, $M_{SUSY}$. This radiative breaking generates a massive $X$ boson with a characteristic mass proportional to $\alpha_X^{1/4}$ times $M_{SUSY}$, where $\alpha_X$ denotes the $U(1)_X$ coupling constant. Furthermore, the spontaneous breaking of the $R$-symmetry in this framework yields a massive goldstino and a massive Raxino. The mass of the Raxino scales with $M_{Pl} \times (B_\mu/M_{Pl})^{1/2}$, where $B_\mu$ represents the mass parameter in the soft-breaking Lagrangian. Additionally, we present a phenomenological analysis of these new particles and offer a cosmological examination of the dark matter content. This study forms part of a series detailing the phenomenology of the minimal $U(1)_X$ model under dark matter constraints. In this context, we derive the mass range for the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson as $M_X \lesssim 100~{\rm TeV}$, dependent on the parameters $M_{SUSY}$, $B_\mu$, and $\alpha_X$, as well as the dark matter candidate mass. This limit constrains the $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling constant. Consequently, we determine the parameter space for the dark matter candidate mass as $100~{\rm GeV} \lesssim m_{\rm dm} \lesssim 10~{\rm TeV}$. These findings will facilitate the design of experimental searches for these extra particles. Additionally, the resulting parameter space can help elucidate the nature of the electroweak phase transition. This work aims to investigate the cosmological implications of these $M_{SUSY}$ and $M_X$ values in the context of baryogenesis. Finally, our analysis of the Raxino mass in the light of LHC data constrains its mass range to approximately 100 TeV. These results will guide the search for these additional particles at the Large Hadron Collider. In this model, a thermally produced scalar dark matter candidate emerges from the sum of two scalar fields, one associated with each of the two generations of leptonic doublet Yukawa couplings. Our scenario utilizes a minimal extension of the Standard Model, consisting of a single triplet fermion and one real dark matter scalar, which predicts a relatively heavy right-handed neutrino ($m_{N_1} \sim 10^{10}$ GeV) and a Yukawa coupling ($Y_{Y_1}$) significantly exceeding the second-generation counterpart ($Y_{Y_2}$). During leptogenesis, the dominant contribution to the baryon asymmetry of the universe (UBA) arises from the interference between the standard contribution from $Y_{Y_1}$ and the dark matter-induced asymmetry. This intersection of the UBA and the dark matter relic density allows us to determine viable parameter ranges for the UBA and thermal dark matter production. Consequently, we predict distinct signatures for the dark matter sector, leptonic sector, and neutrino mass, offering testable implications for future experimental searches. Notably, the predicted dark matter mass falls within the 200–1000 GeV range, making it accessible to LHC searches in the near future. Furthermore, the predicted see-saw mass for $N_1$ is well within the reach of the proposed PTOLEMY experiment, while the predicted mass for $N_2$ aligns with the upper bound established by T2K. The model's prediction for the neutrino mass hierarchy remains ambiguous, whereas the triplet neutrino mass spectrum is tightly constrained, and the predicted scale of the leptonic seesaw mass is significantly higher than that of the dark matter sector. The dominant source of uncertainty in determining the UBA is the dark matter induced term in the decay width of $N_1$, whereas the leading uncertainty in calculating the relic density stems from the annihilation cross-section of the dark matter candidate into $Z$ bosons. Finally, we discuss the model's novel prediction regarding the isospin asymmetry in the dark matter annihilation cross-section, which could be tested by current or future collider experiments. The algorithm's parameters are initialized based on a limited set of prior simulation data, after which the learned control policy is evaluated through data-driven benchmark tests. Our results demonstrate that the degree of control performance improvement can be readily estimated for linear time-invariant systems, while for highly nonlinear, highly excited, and unstable systems, this relationship becomes problematic. Consequently, we offer recommendations for designing effective exploration strategies applicable to both simulation and operation phases. Notably, our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, extensive exploration is unnecessary for many nonlinear and excited systems, even in unstable configurations, as they may achieve near-optimal performance with merely a few trajectories. These insights are derived from extensive numerical experiments and subsequent discussions. Furthermore, we emphasize that the proposed methodology is broadly applicable to data learning tasks in control via standard function approximators. By performing a limited number of trials—whether simulated or experimental—and storing data points rather than full trajectories, the learned control policy can be formulated as the solution to a black-box optimization problem, such as a trust-region quadratic program. This approach ensures that the system's true dynamics remain unknown while still delivering high control performance. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential for achieving substantial control performance gains with minimal effort, given reasonable conditions, through data-driven learning control, provided that only a small number of experiments or tests are required. Additionally, we illustrate that the proposed method is suitable for both offline and online applications. Finally, it is argued that this method represents a viable pathway for industry adoption, facilitating the transition from model-based to data-driven control frameworks. Wess-Zumino-Witten models built upon conformal affine algebras. Defined only for generic levels, their construction involves significant intricacies that lead to numerous formal issues. This thesis identifies the correct concepts for conformal fields, their operator product expansions, and operator insertions within Toda field theory. It presents a framework designed to address integration problems, specifically addressing the two-dimensional path integral definition of the trace of the operator product of two scalar fields. This specific problem was previously unresolved in the context of Toda field theory. Within this approach, the expectation value of the aforementioned operator product is formulated as a path integral over measures, which are explicitly defined as Wiener measures on specific spaces of contours. Consequently, these measures serve as the correct generalization of the Lebesgue measure for conformal fields in Toda field theory. Furthermore, the theory addresses potential divergences arising from operator insertions; suitable countermeasures, analogous to conformal factorization, ensure that such divergences are successfully eliminated. Ultimately, this methodology provides robust and well-defined tools for conducting physical calculations in conformal field theories beyond the Wess-Zumino-Witten model. We propose a GAN-based text generation framework that produces sequences of any length with balanced diversity and realism. By treating text generation as a supervised learning problem between an encoder and a decoder, we utilize a large corpus of human-written texts to pretrain both components. The decoder is then converted into an unsupervised GAN, trained in a self-supervised manner to produce original-quality text. Unlike BERT, which generates repetitive and redundant text, GGAN maintains high perplexity, resulting in more fluent and varied outputs. Additionally, our model produces novel sentences and ideas not present in the training data, an capability absent in the BERT. These GANs are easily fine-tuned for specific domains and tasks while retaining their general capabilities, making them suitable for real-world applications. This research represents a significant step toward general AI that can read, write, and comprehend any language. The primary technical hurdle for TF-QKD remains intensity noise in detection circuits caused by signal reflections between twin fields. Although twin-UNB-QKD was previously suggested to eliminate this noise by interfering all twin states at the middle, it suffers from reduced key rates due to standard preparation and measurement noise. To leverage the noise-immune advantages of twin-UNB-QKD while enhancing key rates, we introduced a hybrid-encoding TF-QKD protocol featuring two twin states. In this scheme, one twin state is prepared via single-photon subtraction from a coherent state, while the other uses the standard balanced Bell-state method. This study presents an experimental validation of hybrid-encoding TF-QKD, achieving a key rate approximately twice that of balanced-Bell-state TF-QKD with twin photons drawn from balanced Bell states. These results confirm the feasibility of enhancing secret key rates through hybrid encoding and provide a foundation for future practical implementations. Additionally, by treating the single-subtraction state as a weak coherent state, we demonstrate that weak-coherent-state-based hybrid-encoding TF-QKD can surpass the PLOB limit over standard optical fiber. This finding not only verifies the PLOB limit but also opens a new pathway for practical TF-QKD applications. Furthermore, since weak-coherent-state-based hybrid-encoding TF-QKD removes the need for high-detectivity photon-number-resolving detectors, it offers an alternative approach to practical TF-QKD. Finally, we explore the possibility of applying hybrid-encoding strategies to other quantum protocols beyond TF-QKD. In summary, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate hybrid encoding for TF-QKD, establishing a significant step toward practical implementation. This strategy holds broad potential for advancing various quantum technologies. Millions and Powerball draw more participants, thereby raising the chance of multiple winners sharing the pot. Consequently, these shared jackpots are split, reducing the net value for individual buyers. This study presents the first application of clustering, specifically the Falcon and Johnson algorithm, to identify cities likely to produce multiple winners. By applying this method to historical draw results, the system predicts successful locations when given a set of cities. The model is tested on historical data from 2016 through 2021. Furthermore, the study establishes a methodology to quantify the benefit of discovering new winning cities while accounting for the risk of claiming a prize that is subsequently shared. The final section outlines a potential strategy for an optimal foraging agent, demonstrating with specific examples how this approach can increase net utility. Ultimately, this technique enhances predictions of successful cities and underscores the value of applying operations research and artificial intelligence to identify opportunities within the chance games industry. Finally, the analysis reveals the significance of using foraging strategies to maximize net benefits from shared jackpots. This work serves as a pilot study for more comprehensive future research. All findings, calculations, and formulas are based on real-world empirical data, while the proposed applications remain prospective. In these experiments, researchers can readily prepare states with significant angular momentum and examine quantum phase transitions by precisely adjusting external parameters. This study extends the large-charge expansion into the strong-interaction regime to analyze Fermi gases supporting charged quantum Hall states. We provide analytical insights into many-body localization, self-bound droplets, topological droplets, and anyonic quasiparticles. Notably, our findings align with recent ultracold atom simulations and provide essential insights into recently observed self-bound quantum Hall droplets. Moreover, we demonstrate a novel class of self-bound anyon droplets that represent stable intermediates between charge separation and fractionalization. While agents often align with others sharing similar characteristics and values, they may overlook potential, albeit less optimal, partners. To enhance overall welfare, we propose that stable agents—those with high value and few preferred partners—should act as matchmakers. These agents facilitate connections between unstable agents, such as pairing an agent with two high positive values with one of two low positive values. We develop a mechanism enabling matchmakers to distribute tasks, welfare incentives, information, and coordination capabilities to maximize global welfare. However, high-energy, pulsed CO$_2$ lasers used for high-velocity drilling often violate these conditions, necessitating a model that incorporates heat diffusion via parabolic rays and accounts for boundary conditions at fluid boundaries. To validate this approach, we measured temperature distributions in water and glycerol around drilled cavities and compared these experimental results with propagation losses derived from both the adiabatic and heat-diffusion models. Our findings confirm that the proposed model, which integrates heat diffusion, accurately describes propagation in such highly disturbed fluids. We observed that temperature distributions follow a $T\propto r^{-4/3}$ law, causing heat diffusion to significantly influence the self-focusing of laser beams in pulsed propagation. This enhanced heat diffusion accelerates the convergence of parabolic rays and shifts the diffraction length inward. Furthermore, this model predicts that beam radius scales with $z^{1/3}$ rather than the standard $z^{1/2}$ found in non-diffusive scenarios. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that during pulsed laser propagation and highly disturbed fluid conditions, adiabatic ray tracing becomes invalid, and self-focusing must be treated as heat diffusion along parabolic rays. This insight is critical for optimizing energy deposition in diverse applications, including fluid drilling, laser-induced plasma channel generation, and laser wakefield acceleration. Additionally, these findings offer a pathway to design optical traps that exploit thermal effects to achieve stronger confinement. While codebase changes reflect these interactions objectively, they offer only a limited view of the actual processes, which are more accurately captured through methods like surveys, interviews, and observations. This study investigates how to enhance developers' sense of awareness regarding the frequency and patterns of these interactions and their impact on development outcomes. To address this, we introduce various code review-centric senses and propose two novel metrics: the review speed index (RSI) and the review participation index (RPI). Furthermore, we gathered data from 2,572 pull requests across seven projects between 2014 and 2017, linking each request to developer survey scores. Analysis reveals that low RSI and high RPI values correlate with higher survey scores when controlled for other factors, suggesting that developers with quicker and less widespread review experiences tend to feel more confident and satisfied. Additionally, survey results indicate that developers with slower review experiences and broader participation feelings exhibit greater resilience to distractions and higher creativity. These findings provide valuable insights for managers and tool developers aiming to foster developers' awareness, confidence, and related skills. Pull request review serves as a valuable mechanism for team members to exchange knowledge, ideas, and experiences, thereby deepening their understanding of the system and enhancing their skills. This paper focuses on two critical processes: how developers choose to spend their limited time during these exchanges and how they perceive these experiences. Specifically, we examine: (1) the characteristics and behaviors of pull requests and their developers; (2) the concepts and metrics defining pull request senses; (3) the impact of these senses on developers' related skills; and (4) the potential for future research in this area. Our research makes the following contributions: (1) We propose two metrics, RSI and RPI, to represent the "sense" pulled by developers when engaging in pull request activities. (2) We analyze the behaviors of pull requests to measure the "pull request sense," demonstrating that developers with lower RSI and higher RPI exhibit greater creativity and confidence. (3) These findings suggest that managers and development tools should encourage flexible and participatory code review behaviors to effectively pull pull request "senses," thereby promoting the development of developers' creative and confident skills. (4) We outline potential future research directions in this field. Our study provides valuable insights into the behaviors and experiences of developers engaged in pull request activities. Within this model, sleptons act as dark matter partners, while charginos are dark matter candidates generated through pair annihilation into sleptons, facilitated by a nearly-degenerate chargino-slepton coannihilation region. We determine the most significant experimental constraints on the model, primarily deriving from LHC searches for balanced di-lepton final states characterized by substantial missing transverse energy. These searches concentrate on events with two same-flavor, oppositely charged leptons, typically representing either muons or electrons/pions. The constraints are most stringent where charginos possess a mass near 650 GeV, corresponding to slepton masses approximately 15 MeV heavier and production cross-sections comparable to the current LHC limit of 25 fm/ct. These findings represent the first constraints on this specific model; future sensitivities will significantly improve with enhanced chargino-slepton mass splittings and higher integrated luminosities. Furthermore, we conclude by outlining the region of parameter space capable of satisfying both dark matter and LHC constraints, which remains viable despite the established 95% confidence level LHC limits. Our results indicate that the most restrictive cross-section limits apply to chargino-slepton mass splittings of 15 MeV or less, aligning with current LHC search capabilities and remaining robust against current dark matter detection experiments. The primary remaining constraints stem from Fermi searches for excess neutral current interactions and potentially from the observed diffuse 140 MeV gamma-ray spectrum. Specifically, Fermi constraints could reduce the viable cross-section by a factor of ten or more, thereby eliminating the majority of the previously viable parameter space. The impact of diffuse gamma-ray searches remains uncertain and would depend on the discovery of a plausible spectral explanation for the 140 MeV gamma-ray flux. Consequently, we recommend that upcoming neutral current Fermi searches above 100 MeV prioritize chargino-slepton annihilation into dark matter. Additionally, we note that if the 140 MeV gamma-ray signal is not definitively confirmed by future observations, the mass and parameter space for this specific chargino-slepton model will be largely excluded. a lattice-based kinetic model known as the Shakhov model has emerged as a promising alternative. In this framework, the Boltzmann equation is substituted with a kinetic equation featuring a linearized collision operator. This paper introduces a simplified kinetic scheme based on the Shakhov model, utilizing a spatial discretization based on a truncated lattice. The resulting trapezoidal integration rule reduces the computational cost of the collision term to the level of the streaming term. The scheme's consistency is verified through numerical experiments comparing it against the Boltzmann equation for flows without walls. This work serves as the first step toward applying the scheme to real-world problems. Although the results demonstrate that the scheme captures the Maxwellian distribution's characteristics and is free from spurious oscillations, they also reveal the presence of the Gibbs phenomenon near the Maxwellian peak, indicating the need for further refinement. Consequently, we propose interpreting the scheme as a macroscopic model for gas microstructure rather than strictly as a discretization of the Boltzmann equation. This interpretation offers a pathway to developing more efficient numerical methods and enhancing the accuracy of simulations. Consequently, we conclude that the Shakhov model holds significant promise for gas flow simulations. However, future research must address the potential for the scheme to lose mass and momentum due to the trapezoidal collision operator's lack of conservation. Furthermore, additional investigations are required to understand the physical origins of the Gibbs phenomenon, its impact on simulation accuracy, and the optimal value of the relaxation parameter to minimize this effect. Resolving these issues is essential for effectively employing the Shakhov model across various flow simulation scenarios. This study investigates how the Coriolis force affects rotationally induced convective motions in the stellar interiors of main-sequence magnetic Ap stars. Based on the assumption of local isotropic turbulence, we employ the local mixing length theory to model convective motions under the impact of magnetic fields. We subsequently construct a toy model of the interior of 10 Cnc, a prototypical magnetic Ap star, by integrating this convective motion model with Ohmic diffusion and dynamo equations. To capture the physics of convective motions, the turbulence magnetic diffusivity incorporates magnetic field gradients and the Coriolis force via their mean effect, represented by the Taylor number. Our findings indicate that the Taylor number, defined as the ratio of Coriolis to inertial forces, can reach very high values in both the radiative and ionized helium zones of 10 Cnc. Furthermore, we observe that the dynamical magnetic diffusivity is significantly suppressed by both the extensive radial distributions of magnetic field gradients and high Taylor numbers. These results suggest that the dynamical generation and transport of ap magnetic fields through ionized helium layers and above are highly inefficient, and consequently, these regions are unlikely to be the sites of the dynamo mechanisms responsible for generating ap magnetic fields. However, we also demonstrate that the dynamo mechanism for τ Boötes-type stars may be viable. Finally, we show that the ionized helium layer in 10 Cnc is too thick to allow the efficient transport of dynamical magnetic fields, yet this layer may be suitable for the generation of slow dynamo-type ap magnetic fields due to its low Taylor number. These outcomes suggest that the mechanisms responsible for the generation of ap magnetic fields in slow-rotating magnetic B and Ap stars differ from those in fast-rotating Ap stars. Furthermore, we find that the transition from fast to slow rotation occurs at a critical Taylor number, which is significantly lower than the value observed in both 10 Cnc and τ Boötes. This suggests that the transition from fast to slow rotation in Ap and Bp stars is not driven by the suppression of ap magnetic field generation under the strong Coriolis force effect. In summary, this paper demonstrates that the underlying physics of rotationally induced convective motions in Ap and Bp stars is quite complex, and we hope that these findings will stimulate further research. constructing state observers for nonlinear systems remains challenging. Traditional approaches, including Kalman-Bucal and Extended Kalman filters, suffer from high computational costs and require precise system models. Furthermore, finite-time convergence is typically achieved only through complex discontinuous estimation algorithms that become ineffective when system uncertainties are present. Furthermore, ensuring finite-time convergence often relies on specific convergence parameters. This paper presents a parameter-free, fully continuous finite-time observer designed to address these limitations. Leveraging the cascading property of double-integrator-like systems, we introduce a slowly-varying transformation to achieve robust finite-time observation without requiring a known upper bound on system parameters. This transformation serves as a robust observer design technique applicable to broader robust control challenges. The proposed method eliminates the need to derive specific system parameters, thereby reducing computational burden compared to previous parametric techniques. Additionally, we extend this technique to develop a high-gain adaptive estimator that achieves both adaptive estimation and observation, further enhancing robustness. Finally, simulation studies are included to demonstrate the effectiveness of this parameter-free design.
