Unlike traditional hand-crafted models, RVFP is learned automatically by exploiting two distinct types of demonstrations: trajectories where the robot fails to reach the goal and those where it succeeds. Each data point consists of a state-reward pair, specifically formatted as a four-dimensional vector: [robot joint angles, end-effector task position, reward for reaching the goal, and reward for following the goal path]. The underlying rationale is that the robot's movement direction, or reaction vector, is primarily driven by the reward signal embedded in its end-effector movement. To improve sample efficiency, the work also incorporates reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on the Amazon Robotics dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, the code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate future research and development. the demand for high-speed, high-quality video streaming. However, current video transmission standards are constrained by the limited capacity of wireless channels and transmission protocols. To address this limitation, integrating video transmission into reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS)-enabled environments offers a promising avenue to expand coverage and enhance system performance. This approach leverages wireless reflections to cover remote areas and improve link reliability. Despite these advantages, RIS-assisted video transmission faces challenges related to the RIS's passive nature, the RIS's inability to differentiate between individual users, and the lack of research on joint optimization involving RIS configuration, user scheduling, and power control. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes a joint design solution for RIS-aided video transmission. The proposed method combines joint user scheduling and power control with RIS optimization to enhance overall system performance. By employing 3D grid search space division, the approach efficiently mitigates RIS passivity constraints. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme reduces power consumption while delivering improved quality of service. Furthermore, it achieves performance gains of up to 100% in both rate and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) under specific conditions. These findings indicate the substantial potential of the proposed solution. In conclusion, this work offers an efficient design methodology for RIS-aided video transmission systems. medical diagnostics for analyzing internal body structures. As a type of projection tomography, a CT scanner acquires X-ray attenuation data at various angles and employs the Radon transform and Radon inversion algorithms to reconstruct the organ's two-dimensional cross-sectional image. These reconstructed images serve as critical diagnostic tools for identifying both normal anatomical features and pathological conditions. This paper presents a novel application of a computer vision technique known as Hough transformation to address the longstanding problem of "peak picking" in computed tomography—a task that has historically relied on heuristics and rule-based methods. Through both simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that applying the Hough transform to the first derivative of a one-dimensional computed tomography signal effectively determines the coordinates of gamma-peaks within sinusoidal functions. Consequently, this approach significantly enhances the accuracy of gamma-camera and single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) instruments in calculating the effective energy window and reduces the noise present in SPECT images. Furthermore, the resulting code is user-friendly, and its application to CT "wavelet" signals for radioactive isotope identification and SPECT noise reduction is discussed. Keywords: computed tomography, peak picking, Hough transformation. Published in *Applied Spectroscopy and Spectral Analysis*, 2021, no. 1, pp. 32–42. (In Russian). ISSN 2070-5823.

We contrast a local response model, which accounts solely for spill-out, against a quantum kinetic response function that incorporates both spill-out and a response mechanism analogous to nonlocality in bulk metals. Utilizing nonlocal density functional theory, we analyze the effects of the first few core and valence electrons in gold (Au) as the primary model system. Our findings indicate that the radial decay of the electric field near the interface differs when only spill-out is considered. Furthermore, we observe that including electron spill-out and the quantum kinetic response from the first few Au atoms can lead to the resonant enhancement and suppression of gap electric fields. These results are expected to provide valuable insights for the design and optimization of nonlocal devices relying on electron tunneling across metal-metal junctions. Additionally, we propose a method to extract the nonlocality characteristic length for metal surfaces from experimental data. This approach is founded on the significant impact of nonlocality on resonant plasmon resonances in metal-metal-glass-metal-metal structures, allowing for the adjustment of the nonlocality characteristic length to fit experimental results. We demonstrate this design strategy using nonlocal density functional theory and core-auvalence-au angular-decomposed projected local density of states calculations. Our results indicate that the nonlocality characteristic length for Au(111) is approximately 0.25 nm. This methodology is widely applicable to metal-metal junctions, including those involving monolayer graphene. Such designs are essential for harnessing nonlocal effects to achieve resonant enhancements of transmitted currents through multilayer core-auvalence-au hybrid structures. This capability could facilitate the engineering of functional orbitals with specific orbital characters for the controlled regulation of core electron tunneling. Leveraging the high stability of the Core NP method for ab initio nonlocal simulations, we propose a core-auvalenyl Au molecular motif as a functional orbital control motif for metal-metal junctions. By adjusting the thickness of the Au layer in this motif, it is possible to tune the ratio of 5p to 5d core electron contributions to the nonlocal response. This capability offers a means to adjust the angular distribution of transmitted currents through metal-metal junctions. Such an adjustment is valuable for core-electron imaging applications, potentially enabling improved spatial resolution in atom probe tomography and low-voltage transmission electron microscopy. We demonstrate that in these settings, a distinct trade-off exists between diversity and accuracy, influenced by both user heterogeneity and the total number of users. Specifically, we establish a general divergence metric that quantifies user differences and a coverage metric measuring the fraction of unique users served. We characterize the conditions under which maximizing overall accuracy necessitates sacrificing the number of unique users served, highlighting that larger user groups create more significant diversity coverage trade-offs than smaller ones. Furthermore, we define a metric for the size of the largest user group and prove that larger groups lead to less significant diversity coverage trade-offs. Finally, our results indicate that the most balanced diversity and coverage outcome is achieved within a homogeneous user environment. Additionally, we introduce a greedy algorithm designed to simultaneously maximize both coverage and average reward, demonstrating its near-optimality in a regularity class defined by specific user diversity metrics. Through extensive experiments, we validate the algorithm's superiority over baselines in achieving both coverage and accuracy. Our findings offer a clearer framework for managing the diversity-accuracy trade-off in user-specific recommendation systems, aiding practitioners in evaluating the diversity of their user bases and the extent of coverage sacrificed to boost accuracy. This understanding is critical for enhancing user experience in recommendation tasks. Similarly, temporal point patterns involve observing event occurrences with associated occurrence times. In each instance, temporal information serves as a critical feature characterizing the data. Given the ubiquity of temporal data across various fields, there is increasing demand for models capable of accurately describing and predicting it. For example, node activation times in networks can reflect brain regions being activated during tasks or companies being founded within a specific period. Likewise, time series data can represent the expression levels of genes.

However, predicting such temporal data remains challenging. While existing methods utilize time as a single dimension for analysis, they often overlook the correlation between observations at different time points. Furthermore, current approaches typically fail to account for the multivariate nature of temporal data. This paper introduces a graph convolutional network (GConvNet) designed to effectively model and predict temporal data. By representing temporal data as a graph where observations at various time points serve as nodes, we capture correlations between different time points by constructing a time graph. This results in a time graph convolutional network (T-GConvNet) that enhances the prediction of temporal data. The proposed method was evaluated on three datasets: a mammalian gene regulatory network (GeneRegNet), a human brain functional connection network (BrainNet), and a collection of stock networks. The findings demonstrate that our proposed T-GConvNet surpasses existing graph convolutional networks designed for temporal data prediction. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ymkano/GConvNet-Python. Temporale Daten sind Informationen, die in einem zeitbasierten Rahmen erhalten werden. Ein klassisches Beispiel ist Zeitreihendaten, das an jedem Zeitpunkt eine einzige Dimension darstellt. Andere Beispiele umfassen Netzwerke mit aktivierten Knoten, bei denen die Aktivierungszeit jedes Knotens eine wichtige Eigenschaft ist, sowie Netzwerke mit Punkten, bei denen die Erscheinungszeit für jeden Punkt eine relevante Merkmal ist. In jedem Fall ist die temporale Information ein entscheidendes Merkmal, das die Daten kennzeichnet.

This prominence is largely driven by the ability of Health Informatics to rapidly address questions that traditional statistics and machine learning often struggle to answer due to biased and imbalanced data. While Deep Generative Models (DGMs) have proven effective in handling noisy, imbalanced, and biased data—making them a natural fit for EHRs—their application to generate patient profiles and virtual drug targets remains underexplored. This paper introduces the first deep generative model for clinical patient simulation, offering a novel approach to learn the underlying distribution of patient trajectories and individual variations using EHR data. By simulating the trajectory evolution of both real and virtual patients, this model aims to enhance the understanding of disease progression and treatment effects, thereby unlocking new therapeutic treatments and treatment regimens. Furthermore, the model is designed to be easily adaptable for clustering and classification tasks, as well as for modeling the trajectory evolution of drugs and therapeutic treatments. We validate our approach using electronic patient data from the Flatiron Health database, which comprises de-identified cancer patient records from over 700 U.S. oncology practices, to demonstrate its effectiveness in simulating clinical scenarios and estimating the impact of therapies and treatment regimes. The source code will be made publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhengru-wang/ehr-dgm}. To our knowledge, this represents the first deep generative model designed for clinical patient simulation. Through visual comparisons, data distribution analysis, and clinical question answering, our model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. These evaluation metrics highlight the model's data efficiency, its capacity to retain information and dependencies across records, patients, and time in de-identified EHR data, and its potential to uncover hidden patterns in patient records. Consequently, our model holds promise for unearthing novel therapies and treatment regimes for diseases characterized by complex dependencies. Furthermore, the model serves as a valuable tool for drug and therapy development, treatment and surgery simulation, as well as for virtual population and drug target discovery. These capabilities could significantly accelerate the drug development pipeline and offer new avenues for future research. We believe that, alongside its promise for therapy and treatment regime discovery, this model represents a significant step toward unifying Health Informatics and Deep Generative Models. Although several tools currently exist to assist with requirement management, none offer high-quality solutions for automatically generating requirements. This challenge is complex because it involves tasks such as natural language generation, information retrieval, and knowledge graph adaptation. This survey examines existing tools and techniques for automatically inferring or extracting requirements to guide future research. Additionally, we present several features characterizing texts with potential unsupervised learning value and discuss appropriate retrieval methods. We also investigate unsupervised NLP model adaptation for this domain and offer initial recommendations on data collection strategies. Finally, we propose a framework and existing patterns to evaluate inferred requirements. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive survey addressing automatic requirement inference, and we anticipate it will significantly influence the field. The source code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/CUQ-Lab/inference-of-requirements}.

\section{Introduction}
Requirements are essential for structuring knowledge, planning, designing, testing, and maintaining software. They are typically gathered through stakeholder interviews or by analyzing documentation to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the system's purpose and behavior. However, creating and maintaining these requirements is time-consuming and costly, necessitating significant effort to refine, prioritize, trace, manage, and store them. This section outlines selected characteristics of potential source documents to aid in selecting sources for requirement extraction. It also presents a list of features useful for unsupervised learning tasks.

It assumes the DAC has a limited energy budget, with a user in the device network actively harvesting energy through a hybrid protocol combining time division power splitting (TDPS) and non-regenerative amplifying. The primary objective is to maximize the sum EE of both the device and cloud networks by jointly optimizing power allocation coefficients (PA) and the rate splitting factor (RSF). The proposed approach is evaluated against two baseline methods: i) optimizing power allocation coefficients, and ii) optimizing power allocation coefficients and the rate splitting factor independently at each cloud each step. As a result, the proposed scheme outperforms the two baselines. Furthermore, the proposed method relies on fast convergence, requiring no additional energy or computational complexity to implement. Finally, the analysis demonstrates that the cloud's EE is positively impacted by energy harvesting, while the device's EE is only slightly improved. Simulation results confirm the proposed scheme achieves up to a 17.5% increase in cloud EE compared to the baselines. Additionally, increasing the energy harvesting duration or rate proportionally enhances the cloud's EE. Finally, the analysis shows that the DAC is more beneficial for the cloud than for the device. This research effectively addresses the challenge of improving cloud EE within DAC architectures, which is often overlooked. It also offers guidance on designing energy-efficient DAC systems by highlighting the critical role of energy harvesting and the necessity of jointly optimizing power allocation coefficients and the rate splitting factor. Moreover, the proposed scheme is easily implementable in real-world scenarios without extra energy or computational costs. methods have demonstrated significant potential for improving the semantic quality of 3D shape manipulation. However, existing approaches typically manipulate shapes by sampling from the distribution of all possible outcomes, a technique that is inefficient and fails to preserve fine details. To address these limitations, this paper introduces D2D-P, a novel, high-quality 3D shape manipulation method. D2D-P achieves this by regularizing the mapping between input and output manifolds to generate a deterministic and invertible transformation rather than sampling from the output manifold. We provide theoretical guarantees for the invertibility and stability of transformation parameters, ensuring the method's effectiveness. -ray pulse from a free-electron laser can induce structural changes in thin films. This process, known as ultrafast demagnetization, is significant both for observing quantum magnetism and for using structural modifications to enhance X-ray absorption. We demonstrate that soft X-ray pulses can demagnetize rare-earth thin films at room temperature, as shown in experiments using tunable pulses from the European XFEL. The magnitude of demagnetization scales with the number of X-ray photons. Similar to the photoelectric effect, the efficiency of this effect depends on both the thin-realm structure and the X-ray spectrum. Ultrafast demagnetization offers a method to study both demagnetization mechanisms and the link between structure and demagnetization. Furthermore, we present a model predicting demagnetization in thin films near resonances of electric-dipole-allowed transitions. This model accurately describes the experimental results. Additionally, we note that the soft X-ray–induced demagnetization effect is not limited to magnetic materials. For thin films near soft X-ray absorption resonances, X-ray pulses can induce structural changes by altering either the equilibrium atomic configuration or the lattice constant. These findings hold potential for improving X-ray absorption contrast in imaging and enhancing sensitivity in X-ray absorption spectroscopy. Finally, it is important to distinguish this phenomenon from the well-known ultrafast demagnetization caused by femtosecond laser pulses via magnetization flipping. This new effect is orders of magnitude weaker and requires a distinct theoretical explanation. This study investigates the efficacy of transferring both acoustic features and semantic labels in low-resource ASR tasks within multilingual environments. This (2+1)-dimensional spin-fermion model incorporates both Hubbard and exchange interactions among electrons, which coexist with long-range Coulomb forces. By employing the mean-field approach and utilizing the Thomas-Fermi approximation to formulate the potential, we demonstrate that the exchange interaction between electrons drives superconductivity, regardless of the Coulomb interaction strength. This mechanism stems from the pairing of electrons with opposite spins and momenta at a filling level one electron per unit cell. Furthermore, we derive the relationship between exchange interaction strength and critical temperature within strong exchange coupling conditions that support high-temperature superconductivity. These theoretical findings align with recent Thomas-Fermi-based experiments on nodal superconductivity in Sr$_3$Bi$_2$O$_3$, a metallic oxide with a layered structure akin to cuprates. Consequently, our results underscore the capability of the spin-exchange interaction to induce high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and suggest that such a mechanism may be common among metallic systems with partially filled spin and Fermi states. Finally, our theory offers a viable pathway for achieving room-temperature superconductivity through the engineering of exchange interaction. efficient utilization of the radio spectrum. While numerous technologies employ a fixed random access method by assigning a unique channel to each packet, this approach often results in significant bandwidth waste. Conversely, random access methods lack a fixed mapping between packets and channels, causing information loss when collisions occur. This paper introduces a novel and flexible packet scheduling algorithm that mitigates collision risks without compromising bandwidth efficiency. The suggested protocol achieves this by utilizing an optimally determined scheduling matrix to minimize collisions. Furthermore, it employs a optimal collision recovery scheme that minimizes the mean access time for successful transmissions. Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm's proposed benefits in terms of bandwidth efficiency and collision avoidance, along with its simplicity and flexibility. Additionally, the method is scalable for both single- and multi-rate systems, allowing packet data rates to vary based on channel conditions. The paper provides theoretical derivations of the algorithm's properties and concludes that the protocol's performance is superior to both random and fixed access schemes. Finally, the algorithm is applicable to various communication technologies utilizing packet data transmission over wireless channels, such as Wi-Fi, UWB, and ZigBee. The core contribution is the proposal and derivation of an optimal collision recovery scheme and packet scheduling matrix, which together constitute the Optimal Packet Scheduling (OPS) scheme. This scheme first selects a non-zero entry from the matrix and recovers collisioned packets by selecting non-zero entries from the corresponding row of the inverse matrix. Simulation outcomes validate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. Compared to random and random with collision recovery methods, the proposed OPS scheme offers not only bandwidth efficiency but also eliminates access delays and mean access time, as proven by theoretical analysis and simulations. The results show that the OPS scheme reduces the mean access time to nearly zero, whereas fixed and random schemes still incur significant access time due to their nature. Furthermore, the OPS scheme is feasible for single- and multi-rate systems. Compared to the random scheme, the OPS scheme reduces the mean access time by 99.9% in single-rate systems and by 60% in multi-rate systems. Compared to the fixed scheme, the OPS scheme reduces the mean access time by 100% in single-rate systems and by 80% in multi-rate systems. Therefore, the theoretical analysis and simulations confirm the effectiveness of the OPS scheme. In conclusion, the proposed scheme is not only effective but also efficient, feasible, and flexible. Its performance is scalable based on packet data rates and channel conditions, and it is not constrained by specific packet data rates or channel conditions. Thus,

Induced Backgrounds (BIB) caused by in-flight muon decays along the beam line, which can hinder the reconstruction of collision products and create asymmetric background patterns between data and simulation. This study investigates a technique called "circular integration" to suppress this BIB. The method averages hits that are spatially separated by a distance equal to the radius of the Endcap Calorimeter (ECAL), effectively smearing out the exponential BIB profile to produce a more uniform distribution. While a similar approach was previously developed for the ILD detector concept, this work presents a rigorous derivation of circular integration and evaluates its impact on BIB distributions within the MUONPOLY collider simulation framework, specifically for the CuMD detector setup. Results demonstrate that integrating hits within the first 1.5 centimeters radially can reduce BIB contributions by up to 90% across various physics scenarios, though they exhibit complex angular dependencies. Despite these dependencies, simulations of the Di-muon search (H -> μ+μ-) indicate that circular integration improves overall physics performance. Additionally, a simulation of the search for the missing energy signature (H -> μ+μ- + MET) was conducted; circular integration yielded mixed results here, suggesting that further optimization and detailed studies are necessary for physics configurations outside the current default setup. Finally, it is confirmed that BIB levels are sufficiently low for this specific physics case, ensuring that detector performance remains unaffected by residual BIB. Extending this concept to other calorimeter-based muon detectors and developing optimized endcap configurations are recommended for future research. Furthermore, circular integration can be readily adapted for use with data during experiments. As illustrated with MuPoliNLO event data, there is good agreement between circularly integrated simulations and data, and notably, collisions are successfully reconstructed in the ECAL for the first time within the MuonPoly framework. These findings pave the way for analyzing full event data in upcoming experiments. To fully realize these results, additional optimization and the inclusion of other BIB sources, such as hadronic BIB, will be required. This concept is also applicable to endcollecting detectors at other colliders, including HL-LHC, FCC-eh, CEPC, and CLIC-c. Furthermore, circular integration may aid in distinguishing BIB from actual event activity, potentially enabling the identification of events heavily contaminated by BIB that would otherwise be lost. Ultimately, optimizing muon detector concepts through techniques like circular integration will enhance the overall performance of future experiments featuring precise muon identification. A striking illustration of this is how the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transition, which signifies the unbinding of topological charges in two-dimensional systems, is absent in three dimensions. To demonstrate the flexibility of charge configurations beyond topological sectors, we employed quantum Monte Carlo methods to simulate a bosonic phase with charge defects in three dimensions. Furthermore, our proposed topologically constrained quantum Monte Carlo algorithm is applicable to a wide range of problems, including the investigation of the emergent gauge fields associated with the BKT transition. However, for software architects, unit tests can create implicit, inflexible constraints that hinder refactoring and discourage a level of flexibility essential for architectural design. Consequently, creating architecture-specific test harnesses is a vital yet difficult challenge, often involving intricate configurations and dependencies that necessitate deep architectural insight. This paper introduces ArchTest, an innovative, open-source tool designed to automatically generate test harnesses for Java applications. By statically analyzing dependency graphs to extract architectural boundaries, it defines architectural units and constructs implicit test boundaries. Developers then use annotations to add custom, granular units for evaluation. To ensure efficient assembly, the tool leverages native Java test framework capabilities, including annotation processing and reflection. Additionally, ArchTest produces visual representations of architectural units, test boundaries, and individual class test coverage. In an empirical study involving five real-world applications, we assessed the tool's effectiveness, flexibility, usability, performance, coverage, and ease of configuration, confirming its significance for architectural design and measurement. Currently, the source code and three fully functional, open-source example applications are available on GitHub at https://github.com/lemayj/arch_test. ArchTest has been utilized in two software engineering research studies: [1] to investigate architectural effects on software evolution and features, and [2] to evaluate code quality as a metric for architectural technical debt within the SQUAD framework. Our findings indicate that, under ideal experimental conditions, the CE$\Sigma$CC can achieve sensitivity to LFV cross sections as low as $10^{-14}$ pb, which corresponds to an LFV branching ratio of approximately $10^{-27}$. These results remain robust against background uncertainties. Additionally, the CE$\Sigma$CC retains the capability to detect LFV events down to cross sections of $10$ fb across a broad range of $Z$-boson decay channels. The study also examines the impact of $\tau$-lepton lifetime and specific $Z$-boson decay modes ($Z\to \tau^+\ell'^- \tau'$) on the limits. Finally, we have established the relationship between event rates and the LFV mixing angle $\delta_{ij}$, demonstrating that the CE$\Sigma$CC can probe angles ranging from $10^{-30}$ to $10^{-18}$ (in radians), contingent upon the collider's luminosity and the $\tau$-lepton lifetime. However, IBI analysis using either modality faces challenges, including irregular heartbeats, EGG artifacts, and data loss caused by patient movement. This study investigates whether IBI time series derived from both ECG and EGG data exhibit dependence on the level of patient movement. To achieve this, we employ both linear and non-linear techniques. Our findings indicate that among linear methods, both autocorrelation and cross-correlation are effective for stationary time series. When utilizing non-linear methods, only recurrence plot-based approaches show validity. Additionally, IBI distributions generated by either modality are similarly influenced by patient movement. These results provide initial evidence that IBI analysis can help assess the quality of a recorded time series, offering potential applications in home monitoring and telemedicine. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/helios-lab-i5/IBI-Movement-Dependence. This code facilitates the analysis of IBI formed from ECG or EGG data, helping to determine if the recording is of sufficient quality for specific medical applications. By quantifying the dependence of IBI on the level of patient movement, clinicians can make more informed decisions. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that IBI formation from EGG is generally less prone to noise. While the analysis in this paper relies on ECG and EGG data from healthy volunteers, these methods are also applicable to other modality pairs, such as wearable-based ECG and heart rate variability. The dataset employed in this research can be accessed at https://helios-lab-i5.eu/datasets/. Finally, the study confirms that IBI estimation is applicable for general health monitoring in both healthy individuals and patients. In this specific analysis, the reference ground truth for IBI was obtained from ECG data. By extending this analysis to compare reference data from ECG against IBI formed from EGG, we can determine the suitability of EGG for specific monitoring tasks. If EGG proves less accurate, it may be reserved for less critical applications. Conversely, if EGG accuracy is sufficiently high, it could be utilized for more critical monitoring purposes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for future investigations into the specificity of IBi analysis for ECG versus EGG. This efficiency is crucial for accelerating iterative algorithms designed to compute t-SVDs for massive tensors. Leveraging the fast randomized truncation method for sparse tensors, we introduce an algorithm termed {\em Randomized t-SVD} (rt-SVD) that requires only two data passes. We analyze the success probability of rt-SVD in yielding a valid t-SVD approximation, deriving bounds on this probability, and subsequently generalize the approach to create rt-SVD with reduced failure rates. We demonstrate the practicality of rt-SVD by applying it to the massive third-order tensor representing the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) from the BICEP array. t-SVD proves highly effective for CMB analysis, facilitating fast de-noising, de-beamforming, de-striping, and de-lensing, thereby enabling the detection of primordial B-modes indicative of inflation. We show that rt-SVD necessitates just two data passes to successfully yield a tensor singular value decomposition, thereby substantially decreasing computation time and bandwidth requirements. Notably, rt-SVD exhibits remarkable robustness against outliers and functions effectively even when data is missing. We empirically illustrate the performance of rt-SVD on real CMB data, highlighting that the method requires two data passes to achieve approximately 10% signal power. Furthermore, we report the first search for primordial B-modes using CMB data from the BICEP array, successfully achieving two data passes even with foreground contamination. We also present an efficient implementation of rt-SVD on MapReduce systems, Big Data platforms, and Distributed Grids. Finally, we outline the potential of MapReduce infrastructure to process vast CMB maps, suggesting that MapReduce systems currently exist with sufficient node counts to rapidly execute rt-SVD on future CMB experiments. We illustrate the performance of rt-SVD on DASHMAP, a specific MapReduce system. Additionally, we demonstrate that the current CMB data from BICEP can be swiftly processed by MapReduce, thereby setting a benchmark for the processing capabilities required by next-generation CMB experiments. We also show that cloud supercomputing offers the necessary computational power to execute rt-SVD on CMB data. We provide a web-accessible version of the reconstructed CMB maps from the BICEP array, accessible at http://www.astro.pitt.edu/~rt-svd. We argue that fast t-SVD is essential for the BICEP array and similar experiments

is a common challenge in economics. When units react to one another, however, standard methods that rely on randomization within units fail to yield unbiased causal inferences. This paper addresses such issues using data from a field experiment involving peer effects in an online fundraising campaign. We utilize a difference-in-differences approach combined with a network-based method to estimate causal effects on individual unit decisions and decision flows. These effects are further aggregated to produce an overall impact on total donations. Specifically, we correct for indirect treatment effects by comparing the change in decisions and decision flows within treated units against those in control units, while controlling for clustering induced by unit connections. Additionally, we develop a method to estimate bias remaining after this correction and use it to determine how much the decision-based reference in the difference-in-differences estimator must be scaled down to accurately estimate the effect on total donations. The final step involves comparing the aggregated effect on total donations from treated units with a baseline effect observed in control units to finalize the total impact estimate. We demonstrate that this novel framework, which leverages unit interconnections, significantly improves the accuracy of total effect estimates compared to traditional techniques. Using the fundraising data, we find that while the effect on donations per user is negligible, the total effect on overall donations is positive and statistically significant. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating unit interactions when assessing total impacts. This paper introduces a novel, fast, and precise parameter estimation technique for cluster clusters. The method iteratively fits a mixture of a series of one-dimensional stellar population models, each representing a distinct cluster population. By incorporating the tolerance of the underlying spectral synthesis code and utilizing Bayesian estimation, the algorithm reliably quantifies parameter uncertainties. Furthermore, this method proves highly effective for clusters containing significant metal-poor or enriched populations. Consequently, it is particularly well-suited for use within large surveys, thanks to its speed and precision. Future advancements will concentrate on enhancing initial population models and determining parameters for individual stars. This study represents the foundational framework for a broader approach to individual star parameter estimation. While the expected volume of an excursion over a finite interval was analyzed by over a decade ago by Burchard and by 2010, the analysis of dense excursion collections on infinite intervals—specifically random field excursions—remained unexplored. This paper addresses that gap, focusing on the model proposed by the second author in 2017. 1. Introduction and main results

1.1. Background
We consider the continuum percolation model of random field excursions on the two-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. Given a non-negative parameter $V_n$ (the field level) and a "fat" set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ (the inclusion region), a field-configuration is a Borel-measurable function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$. An excursion over $U$ is a connected component of the set $\{x \in U : f(x) > V_n\}$.

This result is achieved by employing equiplanar rank trees, a novel variation of segment trees designed to maintain trees within specific planes and execute queries regarding inter-tree intersections. Our approach extends naturally to handle additional linear preprocessing operations, such as determining edge ranks, which consume O(m log n) time for graphs where m ≥ n. Additionally, the algorithm can be adapted to support margin ranks—defined as rank values leaving k vertices on each side of a vertex v—enabling the construction of segment trees with constant spacing and facilitating Q-substitute queries to report the number of vertices within specific planes or to locate the plane containing a specific rank plane. The underlying data structure, the equiplanar segment tree, supports various path-related operations, including computing intersection ranks for edges connecting vertices on different planes, as well as inserting, deleting, and contracting edges and vertices, all within time and space proportional to (n + m) log n. The design relies on two innovative concepts: the plane shift technique and the cross-substitute technique. The plane shift technique manages the disparity between vertex ranks derived from horizontal and vertical projections, while the cross-substitute technique manages paths that traverse multiple planes, allowing for efficient calculation of horizontal and vertical path lengths as well as the minimum crossing count between two paths as they wind through various planes. The analysis demonstrates that the total time required for these path operations remains proportional to (n + m) log n. These findings hold within the standard word-RAM model using O(n+m) storage words of O(log n)-bit precision. All presented data structures can be parallelized using the CRCPR model to operate in time and space proportional to (n + m) log n / Q, where Q denotes the available processors. Furthermore, the methods can be parallelized across P PRAM clusters, each containing Q processors, to achieve an execution time proportional to (n + m) log n / (SQQ), where S represents the inter-communication latency between clusters. Focusing on sequential graph embedding, our results establish that finding minimum margin ranks for planar graphs can be performed in time and space proportional to (n + m) log n. This methodology is also applicable to planar graph planarization, yielding an improvement over previous best results by reducing the time complexity by a logarithmic factor. Additionally, we provide the first algorithm to compute minimum margin ranks for planar graphs

for observing the valley Hall effect, a transport phenomenon involving electron flow characterized by distinct valley indices. This phenomenon is anticipated to arise from the inherent properties of graphene due to its unique symmetries and topological characteristics. However, numerical simulations often suffer from inaccurate results caused by finite-size boundaries. In this study, we propose a precise method for calculating the valley Hall conductivity of gapped graphene that eliminates boundary contributions. This approach relies on the fact that valley Hall conductivity equals the change in valley-polarized polarization, a concept derived from polarization theory. By applying the modern polarization framework to triangular lattices, we demonstrate that one valley Hall conductivity component and another polarization component are universally conserved across any unitary basis, whereas the remaining valley Hall conductivity component changes by a quantized amount at the boundary. These findings provide a novel theoretical foundation for the calculation of valley Hall conductivity. Furthermore, utilizing this formula, we examine the valley Hall effect in graphene under various breakings of lattice and point group symmetries, revealing that time-reversal symmetric valley Hall conductivity can be non-zero, in contrast to earlier predictions. This work deepens our understanding of the valley Hall effect and offers a highly accurate computational tool for investigating valley Hall conductivity in triangular lattices. Additionally, our theoretical analysis indicates that valley Hall conductivity is closely linked to the quantum anomalous Hall effect. Consequently, this study may advance our understanding of valley Hall physics and enable more effective simulations of valley Hall conductivity within graphene. Furthermore, the findings regarding which valley Hall conductivity components exhibit quantization may have significant implications for future valleytronics applications. In the broader context of band theory, the findings regarding the relationship between valley Hall conductivity and quantum anomalous Hall conductivity are also highly significant. We believe this research will contribute to advancing our understanding of valley Hall physics and the related quantum anomalous Hall effect. While ontologies are valuable for modeling shared knowledge, they often diverge when maintained independently, necessitating alignment to merge into a unified model. Although various methods exist for deriving ontological equivalences, capturing intent and context is challenging. This paper introduces the use of Natural Language Ontologies (NLOs)—a recently developed, simple ontology format expressed in natural language—to support ontology alignment. NLOs facilitate easy encoding of domain context, which is typically difficult to infer automatically. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that utilizing NLOs enhances state-of-the-art performance in ontology alignment. Furthermore, this approach helps developers better comprehend alignment outcomes and refine their NLOs to improve future alignments, thereby promoting continuous improvement. Additionally, NLOs enable developers to express alignments directly within the NLOs themselves. Through a case study, we illustrate that NLOs allow developers to capture nuanced source equivalences, including partial, history-based, and negated equivalences. These NLO-encoded alignments can then be leveraged to improve future alignments and to enrich ontologies with precise, history-aware class definitions. Ultimately, this work Leverages NLOs to (1) improve ontology alignment by providing rich contextual context, (2) help developers understand and refine their NLOs, (3) encode history-aware and partial source equivalences within NLOs, (4) express history-aware and partial source equivalences using refined NLOs, (5) express history-aware and partial source equivalences using the combination of NLO-encoded alignments and refined NLOs. By analyzing public, fine-grained sleep data from 2007 to 2019, we measured individual nightly variations in total sleep time (NST) and weekly circadian rhythms (CSR) for 2.6 million individuals aged 50+ in England and Wales. Our findings indicate that NST peaks on weekends, showing a significant weekend effect (WE) of nearly 30 minutes between Friday/Saturday nights and Monday/Tuesday nights. This WE gradually diminishes with age, becoming negligible by old age. Conversely, CSR are lowest on weekends, with a WE of up to 1.5° between Sunday/Monday and Wednesday/Thursday. The reduction in NST correlates with increased nighttime light exposure on weekends. Furthermore, the interaction between age and the WE reveals that the decline in NST with age occurs more rapidly during the week than on the weekend. These results underscore the persistent impact of weekend NST and provide evidence that both NST and CSR are essential for optimal sleep health. Furthermore, we observe that the average NST and CSR for individuals who died between 2007 and 2019 were lower than those of survivors, suggesting that both week-long NST and daily CSR contribute to mortality risk. Finally, the data from 2020 indicates that lockdown restrictions successfully normalized both NST and CSR across all age groups. Collectively, these findings support the development of personalized NST and CSR guidelines to promote better sleep health and reduce mortality. (See Supplementary Material for additional details.) However, experimental data regarding molecular properties and reaction rate constants are frequently scarce or absent, necessing extensive theoretical calculations. Furthermore, numerous molecules lack observations in astronomical data, making their formation routes difficult to verify and validate. This study aims to measure the rotational transition frequencies of complex organic molecules (COMs) for the first time, utilizing a sub-millimeter wave double modulation diode laser spectrometer. The study analyzes a set of damped wave equations featuring variable coefficients and inhomogeneous sources. Initially, the authors construct complex scaled plane wave solutions for the damped wave equation. Subsequently, they introduce and resolve a hyperbolic least-squares problem aimed at determining the amplitude function associated with complex geometric optics solutions. Finally, utilizing the solution to this least-squares problem, the authors derive an Carleman type estimate. This Carleman estimate is then employed to establish stability results regarding the simultaneous reconstruction of coefficients in the damped wave equation within specific L^2-type anisotropic spaces. Furthermore, the authors leverage the Carleman estimate to prove uniqueness and stability criteria for certain ill-posed inverse problems. These findings are then applied to other inverse problems, including those involving wave equations with potential terms and wave equations characterized by non-linear boundary conditions. Carleman estimates can be derived for a wide range of differential operators. Their utility extends to investigating uniqueness, stability, and determination issues for inverse problems involving partial differential equations across analytic, Sobolev, and L^p-type Sobolev spaces. Additionally, Carleman estimates facilitate the derivation of Carleman inequality and have been utilized to investigate null-controllability for various associated control problems. This paper outlines methods for constructing complex-valued solutions to complex operators and demonstrates how this approach can be used to establish Carleman estimates for both wave equations and elliptic equations. Carman estimates are subsequently applied to address various inverse problems for these operators or elliptic equations. Carleman estimates for higher-order elliptic equations have also been developed to determine coefficients in those equations and to address null-controllability and observability issues for associated partial differential equations. Moreover, Carleman estimates for systems of elliptic equations have been constructed to investigate inverse problems for those systems. The authors of this paper have made notable contributions to the theory of Carleman estimates for systems of damped wave equations. In this context, Carleman estimates have been derived for both homogeneous and inhomogeneous cases. Additionally, Carleman estimates have been applied to investigate inverse problems for several related operators and operators with similar structures. By training meta-models on the distributions of diverse prior tasks, meta-learning aims to enhance adaptability to unseen tasks. The primary objective of meta-learning research is to derive parameterization-free representations from mathematical principles or optimization trajectories, thereby facilitating more natural training objectives. However, these objectives rely on task distributions that are often unknown or highly complex. This work proposes a general framework grounded in information theory to explicitly regularize task adaptability during training. Within this framework, the training objective is reformulated as a function of various information-theoretic metrics, such as mutual information and prediction uncertainty. We subsequently investigate specific instances of this framework, deriving learning rules based on these metrics to explicitly optimize for greater task adaptability. Extensive experiments on both synthetic datasets and real-world benchmarks confirm that our framework effectively promotes parameterization-free adaptability. More importantly, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing learnable meta-learning approaches, particularly in scenarios involving tasks that are significantly distant from the training distribution. This indicates that, unlike other methods, our approach is well-suited for applications requiring extreme task adaptability. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhengliu01/meta_info_theory.

This study examines the well-posedness of problems featuring nonlinear memory terms and nonlinear boundary conditions, ultimately deriving new existence results. Notably, in certain scenarios, we demonstrate that solutions to the problem with nonlinear boundary conditions converge to a solution of a related problem that includes a bulk reaction term. Under conditions of ultrastrong coupling between electrons and the cavity's electromagnetic field, vacuum fluctuations induce the dynamical stabilization of quasielectrons that would otherwise be unstable. This study examines the energy loss patterns resulting from the collision of a quasielectron with the stabilized state of the vacuum. Furthermore, we analyze how these ultra-high-energy loss signals depend on the barrier parameters and suggest investigating this phenomenon in future experiments. Our results demonstrate that the final state produced by VSV reliably indicates the true separability status of the initial input. We provide a rigorous lower bound on the VSV cost function that distinguishes between separable and entangled states. VSV exhibits a linear dependence on the number of qubits and can be executed on near-term quantum hardware. Numerical simulations indicate that VSV outperforms existing methods in both efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, by adapting the algorithm, we can effectively verify $n$-partite entanglement within $n$-qubit states. The VSV has been successfully tested to verify the three-qubit GHZ state ($\vert GHZ \rangle = \vert 000 \rangle + \vert 111 \rangle$) and the four-qubit cluster state. This approach is expected to remain effective even when noise is present, as evidenced by our tests on real noisy hardware. Additionally, we illustrate how VSV can verify the experimental generation of a Bell pair, $\vert \Psi \rangle = \vert 01 \rangle + \vert 10 \rangle$, in a real two-qubit system. In conclusion, VSV is particularly well-suited for the entanglement verification tasks required in the certification of quantum devices. Consequently, precise prediction of these functions is crucial for interpreting in-situ magnetic diagnostics. In this study, we employ the ITC code to investigate the characteristics of Microtearing modes within JET's Q95 limited pressure profile and AFS1740's broad pressure profile. A sensitivity analysis was subsequently conducted on modes with driven frequencies between 20 and 80 kHz. For the JET plasma, magnetic field sensitivity revealed sensitivity regarding Greenwald fraction, while the real eigenfunction was notably sensitive to the qX profile. Regarding AFS1740, results indicated sensitivity to Greene's fraction and a broad qX profile, with the real eigenfunction also sensitive to the safety factor at rational surfaces. A comparison of the results showed no significant differences between JET and AFS1740's real eigenfunctions. Finally, the results were compared with AFS1739, a broad safety factor profile with a driven frequency of 50 kHz, which exhibited good agreement with both AFS1740 and JET. This study demonstrates that real eigenfunction predictions are sensitive to various plasma profiles, and variations in safety factor and Greenwald fraction could alter real eigenfunction profiles. Consequently, accurate plasma profiles are essential for precise real eigenfunction prediction. In future work, plasma profiles will be utilized as inputs to ITC to predict real eigenfunctions, which can then be compared with in-situ measurements. Ultimately, this research aims to aid in understanding the specific contributions of safety factor and Greenwald fraction to real eigenfunction profiles, thereby aiding in the investigation of low frequency turbulence. imizing solution to the ill-posed equation $Ax = y$, where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping from a Banach space $X$ to a Hilbert space $Y$, and $\R: X \to (-\infty, \infty]$ is a strongly convex function. A dual gradient method is introduced to iteratively approximate the solution. Under the assumption that $\rho \norm{A} < 1$ (where $\rho$ represents the strong convexity constant of $\R$), the method converges for any initial point $x_0$. Given the ill-posed nature of the problem, exact data $y$ is typically unavailable, necessitating the use of noisy measurements $y_\delta$ where $\norm{y - y_\delta} \leq \delta$. The paper demonstrates that, by selecting the iteration count appropriately, the method remains stable against these data errors. Additionally, it is shown that if $A$ possesses a finite nontrivial nullspace, appropriate parameter choice still yields a minimum norm solution. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to illustrate the method's effectiveness. These findings generalize recent results found in [22, 23, 24]. Furthermore, for finite-dimensional settings with strictly convex data-fidelity terms, a practical parameter choice rule is proposed. This rule, an instance of the discrete source condition utilized in [10], ensures that the proposed inexact dual gradient method achieves optimal order convergence. This represents an extension of the work in [10] to a broader context. Additionally, the analysis in finite dimensions confirms the method's stability when the range of $A$ is dense within $Y$.

While existing approaches primarily rely on established feature descriptors, such as Auto-Feature, to generate matching costs, they often introduce excessive computational overhead and disregard the inherent geometric relationships between SAIs. This paper introduces a GAN-driven auto-encoder (GAN-AE) designed to learn geometrically consistent features from SAIs across four views. Specifically, we propose a straightforward and efficient self-supervised learning framework capable of utilizing the complete pixel information within SAIs to capture geometric consistency across views and enhance the robustness of the learned features. To facilitate this, a Self-Similarity Loss is introduced to capture geometric consistency within individual SAIs and across views during the loss calculation process. Additionally, a Cross-Similarity Loss is employed to capture consistency between pairs of SAIs sharing the same plane. To effectively suppress artifacts and noise, a Data Augmentation Loss is applied to handle misalignment caused by camera noise. Finally, a Discriminator Loss is implemented within a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework to accurately represent the geometric consistency of the input SAIs and recover corrupted data caused by noise. To further refine the network's robustness, we incorporate a density map generator to better capture scene structures and mask regions unsuitable for depth estimation. Extensive experiments on the HFLO and HFLO-High datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques by significant margins, achieving a 30% improvement in FS-S-SAD scores over Auto-Feature and a 16% improvement in FS-S-SAD scores compared to the MVSNet approach. These superior performance levels are attained with significantly lower computational costs, reducing the FLOPs required by Auto-Feature by 44% and increasing the running speed of MVSNet by 56%. Furthermore, our proposed method delivers notable performance gains over specialized LF depth estimation approaches, such as MVSNet-LF and SAIE-Net, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Among these, the weakly symmetric class includes Cartan-Karlhede-Ahmed-Sen and generalized teleparallel theories, which offer significant advantages for calculation, such as the absence of third-order derivatives in their field equations. However, solutions to these theories often require numerical computation, necessitating simpler analytical models to elucidate the distinctive features of non-Riemannian regimes. This article examines the weakly symmetric class, detailing various theories and solving the generalized teleparallel version under the assumption of a locally anisotropic cosmological model. We demonstrate that this model is viable within the generalized teleparallel framework, revealing that its behavior diverges markedly from that predicted by Riemannian gravity. Furthermore, we highlight that our solutions are not restricted to cosmological applications and can be extended to stationary spacetimes. Ultimately, we argue that these analytic findings for generalized teleparallel gravity are also applicable to other weakly symmetric gravities, thereby facilitating a deeper investigation into the unique properties of non-Riemannian cosmological models. Ultimately, this paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of the potential to derive a consistent theory of quantum gravity. Furthermore, we have made these findings publicly accessible through the arXiv repository at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.07360. By amending its transmission protocol, this approach enhances data rates, boosts spectrum efficiency, and lowers co-channel interference. The study evaluates system throughput and spectral performance under power, bit, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) constraints. To ensure fairness among users, a proportional fairness (PF) scheduling policy is adopted, with an approximation method introduced to simplify the computation of the product of sum terms. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms traditional single-input single-output (SISO) WiFi, offering up to a 30% throughput boost in high SNR environments while halving spectrum usage. Furthermore, an analytical model based on this scheme is developed and validated against WiFi 4, 5, and 6 standards, analyzing the impact of channel gain, noise, subcarrier count, and symbol duration on network capacity. Finally, an $O(N^3)$ algorithm is introduced to optimize transmission parameters and predict PF user throughput, capable of delivering optimal solutions for small to medium-sized networks. This research is particularly relevant to product developers and system architects focused on enhancing the performance and efficiency of home WiFi systems. Additionally, algorithm designers may utilize this proposed methodology, which has been refined through extensive simulation, to develop efficient wireless network algorithms.
